units.1.6: Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts

outcomeText.al-l01-o1: know what is meant by the term abstraction
outcomeText.al-l01-o3: understand why abstraction is needed in computational thinking

stations.name: Computational thinking
teaches: Computational thinking is how you approach a problem so a computer can solve it.
It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.
They are used together, not one after the other.

stations.name: What abstraction is
teaches: Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
What is left is a model: simpler than reality, and good enough to work with.
What counts as unnecessary depends entirely on the problem you are solving.

stations.name: A worked example
teaches: A school register needs a name, a form group and present or absent.
It does not need eye colour, shoe size or favourite subject.
Adding unnecessary data makes the system slower, larger and harder to keep correct.

stations.name: Models of the world
teaches: A weather forecast is a model: it keeps pressure and temperature, and ignores individual raindrops.
A satnav keeps roads, junctions and speeds, and ignores what the buildings look like.
Every model is wrong in some way. A useful model is wrong about things that don't matter.

stations.name: Abstraction in programs
teaches: A variable name like score is an abstraction: it hides which memory address holds the value.
A subprogram is an abstraction: you call it without needing to know how it works inside.
Layers of abstraction let one person work on a game without understanding the graphics card.

stations.name: Answering abstraction questions
teaches: Say what is kept and what is removed, and why each decision was made.
Link the decision to the purpose of the system.
One mark is usually for an example, so always give one.

outcomeText.al-l02-o1: know what is meant by problem decomposition
outcomeText.al-l02-o2: know the advantages of decomposition when programming
outcomeText.al-l02-o3: know how to produce a structure diagram

stations.name: What decomposition is
teaches: Decomposition means breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems.
You keep splitting until each part is small enough to solve on its own.
The parts become subprograms, modules or separate jobs for different people.

stations.name: Why it helps
teaches: Smaller problems are easier to understand and to get right.
Different people can work on different parts at the same time.
Each part can be tested on its own, and reused in another program.

stations.name: Structure diagrams
teaches: A structure diagram shows the parts of a problem as a tree, from the whole system down.
The top box is the whole problem; each level below breaks the level above into parts.
It is a top-down design: general at the top, detailed at the bottom.

stations.name: Worked example
teaches: A quiz program breaks into: load questions, ask a question, check the answer, keep the score, show the result.
Each of those breaks down further: 'check the answer' needs to compare, mark and give feedback.
The bottom of the diagram is where the code gets written.

stations.name: Decomposition and abstraction together
teaches: Abstraction decides what matters; decomposition splits what is left into parts.
They are used together on the same problem, usually more than once.
Getting the abstraction wrong means decomposing the wrong problem.

stations.name: Answering decomposition questions
teaches: Name the sub-problems: vague answers like 'break it into parts' score nothing.
Say why the split helps: testing, reuse, sharing the work, or understanding.
If a structure diagram is asked for, draw levels, not a list.

outcomeText.al-l03-o1: understand how to solve problems by applying algorithmic thinking
outcomeText.al-l03-o2: be able to identify the inputs, processes and outputs of a problem

stations.name: What an algorithm is
teaches: An algorithm is a sequence of steps that solves a problem.
It must be unambiguous: every step means exactly one thing.
It must finish: a set of steps that never ends is not an algorithm.

stations.name: Algorithmic thinking
teaches: Algorithmic thinking means working out the steps, and the order they must happen in.
It includes spotting when steps repeat, and when a decision changes what happens next.
A solution found this way works for every similar problem, not just one case.

stations.name: Inputs, processes and outputs
teaches: Input: the data the problem needs to start.
Process: what is done with that data.
Output: what comes back out at the end.

stations.name: Working a problem
teaches: Start by asking what the answer needs to be, then what data is needed to get it.
Write the steps in the order they must happen, then check for missing cases.
Test the steps on paper with a small example before writing any code.

stations.name: A worked example
teaches: A game of pick-up sticks: 27 sticks, two players, each takes one, two or three.
The one who takes the last stick loses.
Decompose it, then write the steps: set up, take turns, check for the end, declare the loser.

stations.name: Answering algorithm questions
teaches: Write steps, not prose: one instruction per line.
Use the same names throughout, and say where a step repeats.
If the question gives a scenario, use its words: sticks, players, pile.

outcomeText.al-l04-o2: know how to make a flowchart
outcomeText.al-l04-o3: understand how to construct a program from a flowchart

stations.name: The five symbols
teaches: Rounded box: start or stop, called a terminal.
Parallelogram: input or output.
Rectangle: a process. Diamond: a decision. Double-sided box: a subprogram.

stations.name: Reading a flowchart
teaches: Start at the terminal marked Start and follow the arrows.
At a diamond, read the condition and take the yes or no path.
Stop when you reach the terminal marked Stop.

stations.name: Decisions
teaches: A diamond holds a condition that is either true or false.
Label the two arrows leaving it, usually Yes and No.
Nested decisions let a flowchart pick between more than two outcomes.

stations.name: Loops in flowcharts
teaches: A loop is drawn as an arrow back to an earlier point.
A condition decides whether to go round again or carry on.
Without a way out, the flowchart describes a program that never stops.

stations.name: Flowchart or pseudocode?
teaches: Flowcharts show the shape of an algorithm, which suits explaining it to someone else.
They get unwieldy for long algorithms, where pseudocode is clearer.
Both describe the same thing; the exam may ask for either.

stations.name: Drawing a flowchart in the exam
teaches: Use the right shape for each kind of step: marks are lost for a rectangle where a diamond belongs.
Label both arrows leaving a decision.
Start and stop with terminals, and check every path reaches a stop.

outcomeText.al-l05-o1: know what is meant by the term pseudocode

stations.name: What pseudocode is
teaches: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in a structured, language-free way.
It cannot be run: it is written for a human reader, not a computer.
It lets you plan the logic before choosing a language.

stations.name: Variables and assignment
teaches: A variable is a named place to store a value that can change.
Assignment puts a value into a variable: total = 0.
In the reference language, input is written name = input('...') and output is print(...).

stations.name: Selection
teaches: Selection chooses between paths using if, elseif and else.
The condition uses comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=.
In the reference language a block ends with endif.

stations.name: Iteration
teaches: Iteration repeats steps. A for loop repeats a known number of times.
A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true, and may never run at all.
A do-until loop always runs at least once, then checks.

stations.name: Arrays and subprograms
teaches: An array holds several values under one name, numbered from zero.
scores[0] is the first item, scores[1] the second.
A subprogram is defined with function or procedure and called by name.

stations.name: Reading the reference language
teaches: The exam uses OCR's own reference language, close to Python but not identical.
You are never asked to write in a specific language: any clear pseudocode is accepted.
You do need to read the reference language accurately.

outcomeText.al-l06-o2: understand that it is inefficient but simple and needs no ordering

stations.name: How it works
teaches: Start at the first item and compare it to what you are looking for.
If it doesn't match, move to the next and compare again.
Stop when it matches, or when you reach the end without finding it.

stations.name: Its one great advantage
teaches: The list does not need to be in order.
It works on any data that can be compared, including text.
It is short and easy to program, so mistakes are less likely.

stations.name: Counting the checks
teaches: Best case: the item is first, so one check.
Worst case: the item is last or missing, so one check per item.
On average, about half the list is checked.

stations.name: Why it gets slow
teaches: Double the list and you double the work.
For a million items, the worst case is a million comparisons.
This is why large systems sort their data and use a faster search instead.

stations.name: Writing it down
teaches: Set a flag to false, then loop through every index.
If the item at that index matches, set the flag to true and stop.
After the loop, the flag says whether it was found.

stations.name: Answering search questions
teaches: Name the algorithm and say what it does step by step.
Say whether the list must be in order: for a linear search, it need not be.
If asked to count checks, count comparisons, not loops.

outcomeText.al-l07-o2: know the condition a list must meet for a binary search to work
outcomeText.al-l07-o3: understand which searching algorithm is quicker

stations.name: How it works
teaches: Check the middle item of the list.
If it matches, stop. If the target is larger, discard the lower half; if smaller, discard the upper half.
Repeat on what is left until you find it or nothing remains.

stations.name: The one condition
teaches: The list must be in order, or the algorithm cannot know which half to discard.
If the data is unsorted, it must be sorted first, which takes time.
Sorting once and searching many times is the situation where it pays.

stations.name: Why it is so fast
teaches: Each comparison halves what is left.
A list of 1,000 items takes about 10 checks; a million takes about 20.
Doubling the list adds one comparison, not a thousand.

stations.name: Comparing the two searches
teaches: Linear: any order, simple, slow on large data.
Binary: must be sorted, more complex, very fast on large data.
For a handful of items the difference doesn't matter; for millions it decides whether the system works.

stations.name: Writing it down
teaches: Keep two pointers: left at 0 and right at the last index.
The midpoint is (left + right) divided by two, rounded down.
Move left or right past the midpoint depending on the comparison.

stations.name: Answering binary search questions
teaches: Always state that the list must be sorted: it is usually worth a mark.
Describe the midpoint comparison and the discarding of half.
If asked to show the steps, write down the midpoint checked at each stage.

outcomeText.al-l08-o2: be able to show the steps of a bubble sort
outcomeText.al-l08-o3: know the advantages and disadvantages of a bubble sort

stations.name: One comparison
teaches: Compare the first two items.
If they are in the wrong order, swap them.
Move along one and compare the next pair.

stations.name: One pass
teaches: A pass goes from one end of the list to the other, comparing every neighbouring pair.
After one pass the largest value has moved all the way to the end.
That is why it is called a bubble sort: values bubble up to their place.

stations.name: Repeating the passes
teaches: After each pass, one more value is in its final place.
The algorithm repeats until a pass makes no swaps at all.
A list of n items needs up to n minus 1 passes.

stations.name: Why it is slow
teaches: Each pass makes almost as many comparisons as there are items.
There can be almost as many passes as items, so the work grows with the square of the list size.
Doubling the list roughly quadruples the work.

stations.name: Its advantages
teaches: It is very simple to write, so it is hard to get wrong.
It sorts in place: it needs no second copy of the list.
On a nearly sorted list it finishes quickly, because the first pass makes almost no swaps.

stations.name: Answering bubble sort questions
teaches: Show the list after each pass, not after each swap, unless asked otherwise.
Say which items are being compared.
State the stopping condition: a pass with no swaps.

outcomeText.al-l09-o3: be able to compare the three sorting algorithms

stations.name: Merge sort: splitting
teaches: Split the list in half, then split each half, and keep going.
Stop when every piece holds a single item, which is sorted by definition.
This is the divide part of divide and conquer.

stations.name: Merge sort: merging
teaches: Take two sorted pieces and combine them into one sorted piece.
Compare the first item of each, take the smaller, and repeat.
Keep merging pairs until one sorted list remains.

stations.name: Merge sort: the whole thing
teaches: Split all the way down, then merge all the way back up.
It is much faster than a bubble sort on large lists.
It needs extra memory to hold the pieces, so it does not sort in place.

stations.name: Insertion sort
teaches: Treat the first item as a sorted section of one.
Take the next item and move it left until it is in the right place within that section.
Repeat until every item has been inserted.

stations.name: Comparing the three sorts
teaches: Bubble: simplest, slowest, sorts in place.
Insertion: simple, faster than bubble, sorts in place, very fast on nearly sorted data.
Merge: most complex, much faster on large lists, needs extra memory.

stations.name: Answering sorting questions
teaches: Name the algorithm and describe its distinctive action: swap neighbours, insert into a sorted section, or split and merge.
If asked to show the steps, show the list after each pass or insertion.
Comparisons usually mean 'when does it stop' and 'how much memory'.

outcomeText.al-l10-o1: know what a syntax error is
outcomeText.al-l10-o2: know what a logic error is
outcomeText.al-l10-o3: be able to identify errors in code and suggest fixes

stations.name: Syntax errors
teaches: A syntax error breaks the rules of the language.
The program will not run at all: the translator reports the problem.
Typical causes: a missing bracket, a missing quotation mark, a misspelt keyword.

stations.name: Logic errors
teaches: A logic error follows the rules of the language but does the wrong thing.
The program runs to the end and produces an answer, which is wrong.
Typical causes: the wrong operator, the wrong order of tests, a loop that runs the wrong number of times.

stations.name: Telling them apart
teaches: Ask one question: does the program run?
If it will not run, it is a syntax error.
If it runs but the answer is wrong, it is a logic error.

stations.name: Finding the line
teaches: For a syntax error, the translator usually names the line, or the one just after it.
For a logic error, work through the program by hand with a known input.
Compare what should happen at each line with what actually happens.

stations.name: Suggesting a fix
teaches: A fix should say what to change and what to change it to.
'Correct the error' earns nothing: 'change > to >=' earns the mark.
Check the fix does not break another case.

stations.name: Answering error questions
teaches: State the line number, the type of error, and the fix.
Use the words syntax and logic: the marks are attached to them.
If the question gives line numbers, always quote them.

outcomeText.al-l11-o1: know what a trace table is
outcomeText.al-l11-o2: understand how and why trace tables help with debugging
outcomeText.al-l11-o3: know how to complete a trace table

stations.name: What a trace table is
teaches: A trace table has one column per variable, plus one for output.
You work through the program line by line, writing down each value as it changes.
This is also called a dry run: running the program in your head.

stations.name: Filling one in
teaches: Only write a value when it changes, so the table stays readable.
Work strictly line by line, in the order the program actually runs.
Take loops round as many times as the program does, not as many as you expect.

stations.name: Tracing a loop
teaches: Each time round the loop, write a new row.
Check the loop condition each time before going round again.
The last row shows the values when the loop stops.

stations.name: Tracing selection
teaches: At an if statement, decide which branch runs with the current values.
Only the lines in that branch change anything.
Write down which branch was taken if the table has a column for it.

stations.name: Finding the bug with a trace
teaches: Trace the program with an input you know the answer for.
Compare each value with what it should be.
The first row where they differ points at the line with the error.

stations.name: Trace tables in the exam
teaches: Fill in every row asked for, even if a value repeats.
Put the output in the output column, not in a variable column.
Work slowly: almost all lost marks here come from rushing.

outcomeText.bl-l01-o1: know the symbols for the logic gates AND, OR and NOT
outcomeText.bl-l01-o2: understand the truth tables for AND, OR and NOT
outcomeText.bl-l01-o3: combine Boolean operators using AND, OR and NOT

stations.name: The AND gate
teaches: The output is 1 (true) only if both inputs are 1.
In a Boolean expression: A AND B, or A ∧ B.
Think: 'A and B must both be true'.

stations.name: The OR gate
teaches: The output is 1 if either input is 1, or both are.
In a Boolean expression: A OR B, or A ∨ B.
Think: 'at least one of them is true'.

stations.name: The NOT gate
teaches: NOT has one input, and it reverses it: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
In a Boolean expression: NOT A, or ¬A.
The small circle on the symbol means 'invert'.

stations.name: Symbols and pseudocode
teaches: AND can be written ∧, OR can be written ∨, and NOT can be written ¬.
Programs use the same logic in if statements.
In the cash machine program, the card is present and the PIN matches, so the AND is true.

stations.name: Two-level circuits
teaches: Gates can feed into other gates.
In (A OR B) AND C, the brackets are worked out first: the OR gate feeds the AND gate.
Work from the inputs on the left to the output on the right.

stations.name: NOT and brackets
teaches: NOT is worked out before AND and OR, unless there are brackets.
NOT A OR B means (NOT A) OR B.
NOT (A AND B) means work out A AND B first, then reverse it.

outcomeText.bl-l02-o1: understand how to complete truth tables from one- and two-level logic diagrams

stations.name: Setting out a truth table
teaches: List every combination of inputs. Each input doubles the rows: 2 inputs give 4 rows, 3 give 8, 4 give 16.
Count up in binary: 00, 01, 10, 11.
Then work out the output for each row.

stations.name: Electric circuits
teaches: Two switches in a row (series): the bulb lights only if both are on. That's AND.
Two switches side by side (parallel): the bulb lights if either is on. That's OR.

stations.name: NOT AND, NOT OR
teaches: NOT (A AND B): work out A AND B, then reverse every result.
NOT (A OR B): work out A OR B, then reverse every result.
An intermediate column for the bracket makes this easier.

stations.name: Three inputs
teaches: With three inputs there are 8 rows.
Use intermediate columns for each gate.
(A AND B) AND NOT C: work out A AND B, then NOT C, then AND them together.

stations.name: NOT A AND (B OR C)
teaches: Work out NOT A in one column and B OR C in another.
Then AND those two columns together.
The output is 1 only when A is 0 and at least one of B and C is 1.

stations.name: Four inputs
teaches: Four inputs need 16 rows.
Group the inputs: (A OR B) and (C AND D) can be worked out separately.
Then combine the two intermediate columns.

outcomeText.bl-l03-o1: understand how to create, complete or edit logic diagrams and truth tables for given scenarios

stations.name: From words to logic
teaches: Find the inputs and the output in the scenario.
Look for the words 'and', 'or', 'not', 'either' and 'regardless'.
Decide which parts go in brackets, then build from the inputs to the output.

stations.name: Scenario 1: the shop alarm
teaches: A shop alarm sounds (X) if the door sensor is triggered (A) AND the shop is closed (B).
Whatever the sensors say, it always sounds if the panic button is pressed (C).

stations.name: Scenario 2: the hospital lift
teaches: A hospital lift has two doors (A and B). An alarm sounds (X)...
if either door is still open,
AND either the lift is moving (C) OR it is overloaded (D).

stations.name: Scenario 3: the greenhouse
teaches: A greenhouse heater runs (X) if the gardener switches it on (A) OR the timer starts it (B).
A window sensor (C) normally sends 0.
When a window is opened it sends 1, and the heater must switch off.

stations.name: Editing a diagram
teaches: Sometimes a diagram needs changing to match a new rule.
Check each gate against the scenario, one at a time.
Test your change with a truth table.

stations.name: Reading diagrams
teaches: To write an expression from a diagram, start at the output and work backwards.
Each gate becomes an operator, and each gate feeding another becomes brackets.

outcomeText.ms-l01-o1: understand the need for primary storage
outcomeText.ms-l01-o2: know the difference between RAM and ROM
outcomeText.ms-l01-o3: know the purpose of RAM and ROM

stations.name: Why primary storage?
teaches: Primary storage is memory the CPU can access directly.
Secondary storage is far too slow for the CPU to work from.
Programs and data currently in use are copied into primary storage first.

stations.name: RAM
teaches: Random Access Memory: read and write, and volatile.
Holds the operating system, open applications and the data in use.
Volatile means its contents are lost when the power is switched off.

stations.name: ROM
teaches: Read Only Memory: read-only, and non-volatile.
Holds the boot program, often called the BIOS.
It tells the computer how to start up and load the operating system from secondary storage.

stations.name: RAM vs ROM
teaches: RAM: read and write, volatile, large, holds what's in use.
ROM: read-only, non-volatile, small, holds start-up instructions.
Both are primary storage, and both are on the motherboard.

stations.name: The boot sequence
teaches: Power on: the CPU runs the instructions in ROM.
The BIOS checks the hardware, then looks for the operating system.
The operating system is loaded from secondary storage into RAM, and takes over.

stations.name: More RAM, faster computer?
teaches: If RAM fills up, the computer has to use slower secondary storage instead.
More RAM means more programs and data can be held at once.
Beyond a point, adding RAM makes little difference: the CPU or storage becomes the limit.

outcomeText.ms-l02-o1: understand the need for virtual memory

stations.name: When RAM runs out
teaches: Every open program needs space in RAM.
When RAM is full, something has to move out to make room.
Without virtual memory, the computer would refuse to open anything else.

stations.name: What is virtual memory?
teaches: A section of secondary storage used as if it were extra RAM.
Data not currently needed is moved there, freeing RAM for what is needed.
The CPU can only work with data in RAM, so anything needed must be moved back first.

stations.name: Swapping
teaches: Data moves out of RAM to disk, and back again when needed: this is swapping, or paging.
If the CPU needs something that isn't in RAM, something else must move out to make room.
Every swap takes time, because secondary storage is slow.

stations.name: Why it's slow
teaches: Secondary storage is thousands of times slower than RAM.
Heavy swapping is sometimes called disk thrashing: the computer spends more time swapping than working.
You notice it as constant disk activity and everything feeling sluggish.

stations.name: Avoiding virtual memory
teaches: Install more RAM so more can stay in memory.
Close programs you aren't using.
An SSD makes swapping less painful, but it's still far slower than RAM.

stations.name: Virtual memory in action
teaches: A user has a word processor and a browser open, filling RAM.
They open a graphics app, so the least-used data is swapped out to disk.
Switching back to the word processor swaps it in again, which is why the switch feels slow.

outcomeText.ms-l03-o1: understand the need for secondary storage
outcomeText.ms-l03-o2: know the common types of storage

stations.name: Why secondary storage?
teaches: It is non-volatile, so data is kept when the power is off.
It holds programs and files that aren't currently in use.
It is much larger, and much cheaper per gigabyte, than RAM.

stations.name: Magnetic storage
teaches: Hard disk drives use spinning platters coated in magnetic material.
A read/write head moves across the surface, magnetising tiny areas as 1s and 0s.
Magnetic tape works the same way, but reads in sequence from a long strip.

stations.name: Optical storage
teaches: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs are read by a laser.
Data is stored as pits and lands burned into the surface, which reflect the laser differently.
Discs are cheap, light and portable, but hold relatively little and scratch easily.

stations.name: Solid state storage
teaches: SSDs, USB sticks and memory cards use flash memory.
Data is stored as electrical charge in cells, with no moving parts.
Very fast, silent, durable and light, but more expensive per gigabyte.

stations.name: Inside the devices
teaches: Magnetic: platters, spindle, read/write head, actuator arm.
Optical: laser, lens, spinning disc, pits and lands.
Solid state: controller chip and flash memory chips.

stations.name: Choosing a type
teaches: Magnetic: huge capacity, cheap, but slower and fragile when moved.
Optical: cheap and portable, small capacity, easily scratched.
Solid state: fast and durable, but dearer per gigabyte.

outcomeText.ms-l04-o1: know the characteristics of storage devices
outcomeText.ms-l04-o2: be able to compare devices using those characteristics

stations.name: The six characteristics
teaches: Capacity: how much it holds. Speed: how quickly data is read and written.
Portability: how easy it is to carry. Durability: how well it survives knocks.
Reliability: how likely it is to keep working. Cost: usually per gigabyte.

stations.name: Magnetic: the card
teaches: Capacity: very high, several terabytes. Cost: lowest per gigabyte.
Speed: moderate. Portability: poor for internal drives, moderate for external.
Durability: poor, because of moving parts. Reliability: good while it stays still.

stations.name: Optical: the card
teaches: Capacity: low, from 700 MB to 50 GB. Cost: very low per disc.
Speed: slow. Portability: excellent, thin and light.
Durability: poor, easily scratched. Reliability: good if stored carefully.

stations.name: Solid state: the card
teaches: Capacity: high and rising. Cost: highest per gigabyte of the three.
Speed: fastest. Portability: excellent. Durability: excellent, no moving parts.
Reliability: very good, though cells do wear out after many writes.

stations.name: Head to head
teaches: Fastest: solid state. Cheapest per gigabyte: magnetic.
Most portable: optical and small solid state devices.
Toughest: solid state. Biggest archive on a budget: tape.

stations.name: Justify your choice
teaches: Exam answers need the characteristic and the reason.
'An SSD, because it is fast and has no moving parts, so it survives being carried' scores; 'an SSD because it's better' doesn't.
Mention capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability or cost by name.

outcomeText.ms-l05-o1: understand the suitability of storage devices for certain applications
outcomeText.ms-l05-o2: understand the advantages and disadvantages of devices based on their characteristics

stations.name: How to choose
teaches: Ask: how much data? How fast? Does it need carrying? How long must it last? What's the budget?
Then match those answers to a device's characteristics.
Always justify: device, characteristic, reason.

stations.name: Distributing a film
teaches: Millions of copies, posted or sold in shops.
Each copy must be cheap, light and hold a couple of hours of high-definition video.
Read-only is fine: buyers don't need to write to it.

stations.name: Carrying work home
teaches: Small files, carried in a pocket every day.
Needs to survive knocks and plug into any computer.
Capacity needed is small compared with a server.

stations.name: Music, cameras and consoles
teaches: MP3 player: small, no moving parts, survives movement, so solid state.
Video camera: fast writes and portability, so a solid state memory card.
Console game: mass-produced, so optical disc, or a download.

stations.name: Servers and operating systems
teaches: School network storage: many terabytes, always plugged in, so magnetic hard disks.
A computer's operating system: needs to load fast, so solid state.
Servers often use both: SSD for speed, hard disks for bulk.

stations.name: Long-term archives
teaches: Training videos kept for years: huge capacity, rarely accessed, so magnetic tape or archive discs.
Photo backups: a second copy, kept somewhere else, often an external hard disk or the cloud.
Any backup should be kept away from the original.

outcomeText.ms-l06-o1: know the units bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte and petabyte
outcomeText.ms-l06-o2: be able to convert between units
outcomeText.ms-l06-o3: understand that data must be converted to binary to be processed

stations.name: Why binary?
teaches: Computers are built from transistors, which are switches: on or off.
Two states map perfectly onto 1 and 0.
Everything, from numbers to images and sound, is stored as binary.

stations.name: Bits, nibbles and bytes
teaches: A bit is a single 1 or 0.
A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.
One byte can store one character, or a number from 0 to 255.

stations.name: Kilo, mega, giga
teaches: 1 kilobyte (kB) = 1,000 bytes. 1 megabyte (MB) = 1,000 kB.
1 gigabyte (GB) = 1,000 MB. 1 terabyte (TB) = 1,000 GB. 1 petabyte (PB) = 1,000 TB.
Each step up multiplies by 1,000.

stations.name: Converting units
teaches: Going up a unit: divide by 1,000. Going down: multiply by 1,000.
Bits to bytes: divide by 8. Bytes to bits: multiply by 8.
Watch the capital B: KB is kilobytes, Kb is kilobits.

stations.name: Storing a number
teaches: 1 bit stores a Boolean: true or false, 1 or 0.
A nibble stores 0 to 15: enough for a single digit on an LCD display.
A byte stores 0 to 255: enough for one character, such as A = 65.

stations.name: How big is a petabyte?
teaches: 1 PB is a million gigabytes.
It would hold roughly 250,000 films, or 200 million photos.
Data centres now measure their storage in petabytes and exabytes.

outcomeText.ms-l07-o2: understand how to calculate data capacity requirements

stations.name: What is data capacity?
teaches: Capacity is how much data a device can hold, measured in bytes and their multiples.
To work out what you need, calculate one file's size, then multiply by how many files.
Always check whether the answer is wanted in bits, bytes, MB or GB.

stations.name: Image file size
teaches: File size (bits) = width × height × colour depth.
Width and height are in pixels; colour depth is bits per pixel.
Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kB and again for MB.
Real files also include metadata.

stations.name: Sound file size
teaches: File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration in seconds.
Sample rate is measured in hertz: samples per second.
Stereo doubles it, because there are two channels.

stations.name: Text file size
teaches: File size (bits) = number of characters × bits per character.
ASCII uses 7 or 8 bits per character; Unicode often uses 16.
Spaces and punctuation are characters too.

stations.name: Scenario practice
teaches: Read carefully: what's the file size, and how many files?
Convert at the end, not halfway through.
Show your working: marks are given for the method as well as the answer.

stations.name: Estimating
teaches: Rounding helps: treat 1,024 as 1,000 and 44,100 Hz as 44 kHz.
Check the answer is sensible: a photo shouldn't come out as 3 GB.
Compression makes real files smaller than the calculated raw size.

outcomeText.ms-l08-o1: convert positive denary whole numbers (0-255) to 8-bit binary and back
outcomeText.ms-l08-o3: understand the terms most and least significant bit

stations.name: Place values
teaches: Each bit in an 8-bit number has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Add the place values above every 1 to get the denary number.
The largest 8-bit number is 255, when every bit is 1.

stations.name: Denary to binary
teaches: Work from the left: does 128 fit? If yes, write 1 and subtract it.
Carry on down through 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Check by adding your place values back up.

stations.name: MSB and LSB
teaches: The most significant bit (MSB) is the leftmost bit: it has the largest place value.
The least significant bit (LSB) is the rightmost: place value 1.
Changing the MSB changes the number by 128; changing the LSB changes it by 1.

stations.name: Binary addition
teaches: Add column by column from the right, just like denary.
0+0 = 0; 0+1 = 1; 1+1 = 10, so write 0 and carry 1.
1+1+1 = 11, so write 1 and carry 1.

stations.name: Overflow
teaches: 8 bits can only hold 0 to 255.
If the answer needs a 9th bit, it can't be stored: this is an overflow error.
The stored answer is wrong, which can crash a program or corrupt data.

stations.name: Why it matters
teaches: More bits means bigger numbers: 16 bits reach 65,535.
Programs must choose a data type big enough for the values they'll hold.
Famous failures, including a rocket, have been caused by overflow.

outcomeText.ms-l10-o1: know how to perform left and right binary shifts
outcomeText.ms-l10-o2: understand what a binary shift achieves
outcomeText.ms-l10-o3: convert denary to 2-digit hexadecimal and back

stations.name: Left shift
teaches: Every bit moves left, and a 0 comes in at the right.
A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
Any bit pushed off the left end is lost: that's an overflow.

stations.name: Right shift
teaches: Every bit moves right, and a 0 comes in at the left.
A shift of one place divides the number by 2.
Bits pushed off the right end are lost, so the answer is rounded down.

stations.name: Shifts and precision
teaches: Shifting is very fast, so processors use it instead of multiplying and dividing where they can.
Left shifts can overflow if a 1 is pushed off the left end.
Right shifts lose the remainder.

stations.name: Why hexadecimal?
teaches: Hexadecimal is base 16, using 0-9 then A-F.
One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits.
It's much shorter and easier for people to read and copy than long binary.

stations.name: Denary and hex
teaches: Denary to hex: divide by 16; the whole number is the first digit, the remainder the second.
Or convert to binary first, then split into two nibbles.
Hex to denary: first digit × 16, plus the second digit.

stations.name: Binary and hex
teaches: Split the byte into two nibbles of 4 bits.
Convert each nibble separately into one hex digit.
1101 0110 becomes D6.

outcomeText.ms-l11-o1: know which parts of the topic I am secure on
outcomeText.ms-l11-o2: finish any outstanding tasks from lessons 1 to 10

stations.name: Primary storage
teaches: RAM: volatile, read/write, holds what's in use.
ROM: non-volatile, read-only, holds the boot program.
Primary storage is directly accessible by the CPU.

stations.name: Virtual memory
teaches: Secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full.
Data is swapped in and out as the CPU needs it.
Much slower than RAM, so more RAM is the real fix.

stations.name: Secondary storage
teaches: Magnetic: platters and a read/write head; cheap and huge.
Optical: a laser reading pits and lands; cheap and portable.
Solid state: flash memory; fast and durable but dearer.

stations.name: Units and capacity
teaches: Bit, nibble (4), byte (8), then kB, MB, GB, TB, PB, each ×1,000.
Image size = width × height × colour depth.
Sound size = sample rate × bit depth × duration.

stations.name: Binary and addition
teaches: MSB is leftmost, LSB is rightmost.
8 bits hold 0 to 255; anything larger overflows.

stations.name: Shifts and hex
teaches: Left shift ×2 per place; right shift ÷2 per place.
One hex digit is exactly 4 bits.
A = 10 up to F = 15.

outcomeText.ms-l12-o1: understand that all data, including text, is represented in binary
outcomeText.ms-l12-o2: know what is meant by a character set
outcomeText.ms-l12-o3: understand the relationship between the number of bits and the number of characters

stations.name: Text as numbers
teaches: Every character has a number, called its character code.
The code is stored in binary, like any other number.
The computer uses a character set to know which code means which character.

stations.name: ASCII
teaches: ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 128 different characters.
It covers English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes.
Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 characters.

stations.name: The ASCII pattern
teaches: Codes are in order: A is 65, B is 66, and so on.
Lower case starts 32 later: a is 97.
The digits 0 to 9 are codes 48 to 57.

stations.name: Unicode
teaches: Unicode was designed to represent every writing system in the world.
It uses 16 bits or more, giving tens of thousands of characters.
It includes emoji, and the first 128 codes match ASCII.

stations.name: Bits and characters
teaches: The number of bits decides how many characters can be represented: 2 to the power n.
2 bits give 4; 4 bits give 16; 8 bits give 256.
Add one bit and you double the number of characters.

stations.name: Text file size
teaches: File size = number of characters × bits per character.
The same message in Unicode is roughly twice the size of 8-bit ASCII.
Spaces and punctuation count as characters.

stations.name: Final challenge: spell it in binary

outcomeText.ms-l13-o1: understand how an image is a series of pixels represented in binary
outcomeText.ms-l13-o2: know what is meant by metadata
outcomeText.ms-l13-o3: understand the effect of colour depth and resolution on file size

stations.name: Pixels and bitmaps
teaches: A bitmap image is a grid of pixels.
Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number.
The computer rebuilds the image by colouring each pixel in turn.

stations.name: Colour depth
teaches: Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel.
1 bit gives 2 colours; 2 bits give 4; 8 bits give 256; 24 bits give over 16 million.
The number of colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth.

stations.name: Resolution
teaches: Resolution is the number of pixels in the image, usually written width × height.
More pixels means more detail, and a bigger file.
Doubling the width and height makes the file four times bigger.

stations.name: Metadata
teaches: Metadata is data about the data: information stored with the image.
Examples: width, height, colour depth, file type, date created, camera settings and sometimes GPS location.
Without it, the computer wouldn't know how to display the pixels.

stations.name: Calculating file size
teaches: File size in bits = width × height × colour depth.
Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kilobytes.
Real files are a little larger because of metadata.

stations.name: Quality against size
teaches: Increasing resolution or colour depth improves quality but increases file size.
Choose the lowest that still looks good enough for the job.
A website icon needs far less than a poster.

outcomeText.ms-l14-o1: understand how sound is sampled and stored in digital form
outcomeText.ms-l14-o2: understand how sample rate, duration and bit depth affect file size and quality

stations.name: Analogue to digital
teaches: Sound is an analogue wave: it changes smoothly and continuously.
Computers store discrete numbers, so the wave must be measured at intervals.
Each measurement is called a sample, and is stored in binary.

stations.name: Sample rate
teaches: Sample rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz.
A higher rate follows the wave more closely, so the recording is more accurate.
CD quality is 44,100 Hz.

stations.name: Bit depth
teaches: Bit depth is the number of bits used to store each sample.
More bits means more possible levels, so the amplitude is recorded more precisely.
3 bits give 8 levels; 16 bits give 65,536.

stations.name: Sound file size
teaches: File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration in seconds.
Double any one of them and the file size doubles.
Stereo doubles it again, because each channel is stored separately.

stations.name: Quality against size
teaches: Higher sample rate and bit depth mean better quality and bigger files.
Speech needs far less than music, so phone calls use low rates.
Choose what's good enough for the purpose.

stations.name: In the studio
teaches: Practise reading a wave and choosing the nearest level at each sample.
Then calculate the file size from your choices.
This is exactly what an exam question on sound representation looks like.

outcomeText.ms-l15-o2: understand the difference between lossy and lossless compression
outcomeText.ms-l15-o3: know why some data can only be compressed losslessly

stations.name: Why compress?
teaches: Smaller files use less storage space.
They transfer faster and use less bandwidth, so streaming and downloads work better.
More files fit on a device, and web pages load quicker.

stations.name: Lossy compression
teaches: Some data is permanently removed to make the file much smaller.
The removed detail is chosen to be hard for people to notice, such as sounds outside normal hearing.
The original file can never be recovered.

stations.name: Lossless compression
teaches: No data is lost: the file is rewritten more efficiently, and can be restored exactly.
Patterns and repeats are recorded once instead of many times.
The saving is smaller than with lossy compression.

stations.name: Which one, when?
teaches: Photos, music and video: lossy is fine, and the saving is big.
Text, spreadsheets, program files and archives: lossless only.
Sometimes both: a video may use lossy video with lossless subtitles.

stations.name: Run-length encoding
teaches: A lossless method: instead of storing every pixel, store the colour and how many times it repeats.
001 1011 means eleven pixels of colour 001.
It works brilliantly on images with large blocks of one colour, and badly on noisy photos.

stations.name: Does it always help?
teaches: RLE shrinks images with long runs of the same colour.
On a detailed photo, where colours change every pixel, it can make the file bigger.
Compare the raw size with the compressed size to decide.

outcomeText.ms-l16-o1: know which parts of data representation I am secure on
outcomeText.ms-l16-o2: finish outstanding tasks from lessons 12 to 15

stations.name: Character sets
teaches: A character set links characters to binary codes.
ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters. Unicode: 16+ bits, every writing system.
n bits give 2ⁿ characters.

stations.name: Images
teaches: File size = width × height × colour depth.
Colour depth is bits per pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ colours.
Metadata stores dimensions, colour depth, date and more.

stations.name: Sound
teaches: File size = sample rate × bit depth × duration.
Sample rate is samples per second; bit depth is bits per sample.
Higher values mean better quality and bigger files.

stations.name: Compression
teaches: Lossy: data removed permanently, much smaller files, used for photos, music and video.
Lossless: nothing lost, the original can be restored, used for text and programs.
Run-length encoding is a lossless method.

stations.name: Calculations practice
teaches: Write the formula, substitute the numbers, then convert the units.
Divide bits by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kB and again for MB.
Check the answer is sensible.

stations.name: Exam technique
teaches: Show your working: method marks are available even if the final number is wrong.
Watch the units the question asks for.
Learn the definitions: sampling, metadata, character set, lossy, lossless.

outcomeText.ns-l01-o1: understand the different forms of attack against computer systems

stations.name: What is a cyberattack?
teaches: An attempt to damage or disrupt a system, or to gain unauthorised access to it or its data.
Attacks can come from outside the network or from inside it.
The people who carry them out are often called hackers or attackers.

stations.name: The six forms of attack
teaches: Malware, social engineering (including phishing), brute-force attacks, denial of service, data interception and theft, and SQL injection.
Some attack the technology; others attack the people using it.

stations.name: What do attackers want?
teaches: Money: ransoms, fraud and selling stolen data.
Data: personal details, passwords, company secrets.
Disruption: damaging a rival, making a political point, or simply showing off.

stations.name: CryptoLocker
teaches: CryptoLocker was ransomware that appeared in 2013 and encrypted victims' files.
Victims were told to pay a ransom in Bitcoin to get their files back.
It spread through infected email attachments and a botnet.

stations.name: Operation Tovar
teaches: In 2014, police forces and security companies from several countries worked together to take down the botnet behind CryptoLocker.
The operation was called Operation Tovar.
The FBI offered a reward of up to $3 million for information leading to the arrest of Evgeniy Bogachev, who has never been caught.

stations.name: How much damage?
teaches: CryptoLocker is estimated to have extorted around $3 million from victims before it was shut down.
The cost of an attack isn't only the ransom: there's downtime, lost data, recovery and damage to reputation.
Organisations can also be fined if they fail to protect personal data.

outcomeText.ns-l02-o1: understand the threats of various forms of malware
outcomeText.ns-l02-o2: understand how to identify and protect against malware

stations.name: What is malware?
teaches: Malware is short for malicious software: any program written to damage or gain access to a system.
It can delete or change files, steal data, spy on users or take control of a computer.
It spreads through downloads, attachments, websites and USB sticks.

stations.name: Viruses
teaches: A virus attaches itself to a file or program.
It needs the user to run that file before it can do anything.
Once running, it copies itself into other files and spreads when those files are shared.

stations.name: Worms
teaches: A worm is self-replicating: it copies itself without any user action.
It spreads across networks by finding weaknesses in software.
Worms can spread extremely fast and use up bandwidth and processing time.

stations.name: Trojans
teaches: A trojan is disguised as legitimate software, such as a free game or a useful tool.
The user installs it themselves, and it then does something harmful.
Trojans don't replicate, but they often open a backdoor for the attacker.

stations.name: Ransomware and spyware
teaches: Ransomware encrypts the user's files and demands a payment for the key.
Spyware secretly records what the user does, including keystrokes, and sends it to the attacker.
A keylogger is a common form of spyware used to capture passwords.

stations.name: Stopping malware
teaches: Anti-malware software scans files and checks them against known threats.
Keep operating systems and applications patched and up to date.
Don't open unexpected attachments, and back up important files regularly.
Firewalls and user access levels limit what malware can reach.

outcomeText.ns-l03-o1: understand the concept of SQL injection
outcomeText.ns-l03-o2: understand how to protect against SQL injection

stations.name: Databases and SQL
teaches: Websites store usernames, passwords and records in a database.
SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to ask the database for records, and to add, change or delete them.
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Sam' asks for Sam's record.

stations.name: The dangerous line
teaches: The code in your starter joins the user's input onto the query as text.
Joining a string to a variable like this is called concatenation.
Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL command.

stations.name: The attack
teaches: An attacker types SQL into the text box instead of a username.
Entering ' OR 1=1 -- makes the condition always true and comments out the rest.
The database returns every record, and the attacker is logged in.

stations.name: What attackers gain
teaches: Log in as another user, including an administrator.
Read every record: names, emails, passwords and card details.
Change or delete records, or even destroy whole tables.

stations.name: Stopping injection
teaches: Validate input: check it matches what's expected, such as letters and numbers only.
Sanitise input: remove or escape dangerous characters like quotation marks.
Use parameterised queries, which keep the user's input separate from the SQL command.
Give the website's database account only the permissions it needs.

stations.name: Testing for holes
teaches: Penetration testers deliberately try injection attacks to find weaknesses.
Detailed error messages help attackers, so live sites should hide them.
Old, unpatched website software is a common way in.

outcomeText.ns-l04-o2: understand how to identify and protect against phishing

stations.name: What is phishing?
teaches: An online fraud technique: fake messages designed to trick people into giving away personal information.
The message pretends to come from a trustworthy organisation, such as a bank or a school.
It's a form of social engineering: it targets people, not software.

stations.name: What attackers gain
teaches: Usernames and passwords, which open email, banking and school accounts.
Bank and card details, used for fraud or sold on.
A way into an organisation's network, by stealing a staff login.

stations.name: Spot the signs
teaches: Check the sender's address, not just the display name.
Look for urgency or threats: 'act now or your account will be closed'.
Generic greetings, spelling mistakes and odd formatting are clues.
Unexpected attachments or links asking you to log in.

stations.name: Check the link
teaches: Hover over a link to see where it really goes.
Attackers use lookalike addresses, such as barclays-secure-login.com.
A padlock only means the connection is encrypted; it doesn't mean the site is honest.

stations.name: Targeted phishing
teaches: Spear phishing targets one person, using details about them to look convincing.
Whaling targets senior staff, such as a head teacher or finance director.
Smishing uses text messages and vishing uses phone calls.

stations.name: What to do
teaches: Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages.
Check with the organisation using a number or address you already know.
Report it: to the teacher, the IT team, or a national reporting service.
If you did click, change your password straight away and tell someone.

outcomeText.ns-l05-o2: understand how to identify and protect against phishing
outcomeText.ns-l05-o3: understand the ways people are a weak point

stations.name: People as a weak point
teaches: Human actions cause many security problems: not installing updates, not locking doors, not logging off.
Passwords written on sticky notes, or shared with a friend.
Printouts with personal data left lying around, and attachments opened without thinking.

stations.name: Blagging
teaches: Blagging, also called pretexting, means inventing a story to get information.
For example, phoning the IT desk pretending to be a head teacher locked out of an account.
Attackers research their target first so the story sounds real.

stations.name: Shouldering and tailgating
teaches: Shouldering, or shoulder surfing, means watching someone enter a password or PIN.
Tailgating means following an authorised person through a secure door.
Both rely on people being polite or not paying attention.

stations.name: Baiting
teaches: Baiting leaves something tempting for the victim to pick up, such as a USB stick labelled 'Payroll'.
When it's plugged in, malware installs itself.
Online baiting offers free downloads, prizes or games.

stations.name: Phishing, vishing and smishing
teaches: Phishing by email, vishing by phone call, smishing by text message.
All three use the same trick: pretend to be trusted, then create urgency.
Recorded messages and spoofed caller IDs make vishing convincing.

stations.name: Turning people into a strength
teaches: Training staff and students to recognise attacks.
Clear policies: never share passwords, always lock screens, challenge strangers.
Two-factor authentication, so a stolen password isn't enough.
An acceptable use policy that everyone agrees to.

outcomeText.ns-l06-o1: understand what a brute-force attack is
outcomeText.ns-l06-o2: understand how to identify and protect against brute-force attacks

stations.name: What is a brute-force attack?
teaches: Software tries every possible combination of characters until it finds the password.
No clever trick is needed: just speed, and modern computers are very fast.
It's often automated and aimed at thousands of accounts at once.

stations.name: Dictionary attacks
teaches: A dictionary attack tries lists of common passwords and real words first.
Lists from previous data breaches are used, because people reuse passwords.
'password', '123456' and 'qwerty' are tried within the first second.

stations.name: How long would it take?
teaches: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible passwords.
Using upper case, numbers and symbols increases the choices per character.
A short password can fall in seconds; a long passphrase could take centuries.

stations.name: Password policies
teaches: Organisations set rules: a minimum length, a mix of character types, and no reuse.
Passphrases of three random words are long, strong and memorable.
Password managers create and store a different strong password for every site.

stations.name: Fighting back
teaches: Account lockouts: after a few failed attempts the account is locked or delayed.
CAPTCHA tests block automated software.
Two-factor authentication means a stolen password isn't enough.
Rate limiting slows down repeated attempts from the same source.

stations.name: Behind the scenes
teaches: Websites should store a hash of your password, not the password itself.
Hashing is one-way: you can check a password, but not work it out from the hash.
A 'salt' adds random data so identical passwords have different hashes.

outcomeText.ns-l07-o1: understand what a denial-of-service attack is
outcomeText.ns-l07-o2: understand how to identify and protect against denial-of-service attacks

stations.name: Denial of service
teaches: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack floods a server with requests so it can't respond to real users.
Nothing is stolen: the aim is disruption.
The service slows down or goes offline completely.

stations.name: DDoS and botnets
teaches: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack uses many computers at once.
Infected computers under an attacker's control are called zombies, and the network of them is a botnet.
The owners usually have no idea their device is taking part.

stations.name: 21 October 2016
teaches: A huge DDoS attack hit Dyn, a company that runs DNS servers for much of the internet.
Netflix, Twitter, Spotify, Reddit, PayPal and many news sites became unreachable.
The Mirai botnet was made of hacked smart devices, such as cameras and routers, using default passwords.

stations.name: Effects
teaches: Customers can't reach the service, so sales and trust are lost.
Staff can't work if internal systems are affected.
Sometimes a DDoS is a smokescreen while another attack happens elsewhere.

stations.name: Defending the server
teaches: Firewalls and filters can block suspicious traffic patterns.
Rate limiting caps how many requests one source can make.
Extra capacity and traffic-spreading services absorb large floods.
Intrusion detection systems and monitoring spot attacks early.

stations.name: Watching the attacks
teaches: Attack maps show DDoS traffic around the world in near real time.
Monitoring normal traffic makes unusual spikes obvious.
Many attacks are bought as a service for a few pounds, which is illegal.

stations.name: Final challenge: the anatomy of a DDoS

outcomeText.ns-l08-o1: understand the threat that data interception and theft poses
outcomeText.ns-l08-o2: understand how to identify and protect against data interception

stations.name: Data interception and theft
teaches: Data is captured as it travels across a network, without the sender or receiver knowing.
Attackers can also steal data at rest: from a stolen laptop, USB stick or printout.
The aim is usually personal details, passwords or company secrets.

stations.name: Packet sniffing
teaches: Packet sniffer software captures the packets travelling on a network.
Network managers use it legitimately to find faults; attackers use the same tools to steal data.
Unsecured or public Wi-Fi makes sniffing much easier.

stations.name: Man in the middle
teaches: The attacker sits between you and the service, passing messages on.
Both sides think they're talking directly to each other.
A fake Wi-Fi hotspot, such as 'Free Airport WiFi', is a common trick.

stations.name: What attackers gain
teaches: Usernames and passwords typed into unencrypted sites.
Bank details, private messages and company documents.
Enough personal information to commit identity fraud.

stations.name: Encryption is the answer
teaches: Encryption scrambles data so intercepted packets are useless without the key.
HTTPS encrypts traffic between a browser and a website; WPA2 encrypts Wi-Fi.
A VPN encrypts everything between your device and a trusted server.

stations.name: Other protections
teaches: Don't send sensitive data over open Wi-Fi; use mobile data or a VPN.
Log off, lock screens and shred printouts.
Physical security: locked server rooms and cabinets.
Access levels mean a stolen login only reaches part of the data.

outcomeText.ns-l09-o1: understand the ways people are a weak point in system security
outcomeText.ns-l09-o2: know how penetration testing, anti-malware, firewalls and user access levels help against cyberattack

stations.name: Penetration testing
teaches: Evaluating the security of a system by safely trying to exploit its weaknesses.
It's done with the owner's permission, and the findings are reported so they can be fixed.
Testers act like attackers, including trying social engineering.

stations.name: Anti-malware software
teaches: Scans files and programs and compares them against known malware.
Watches for suspicious behaviour to catch new threats.
Must be kept up to date, because new malware appears daily.
Quarantines or removes anything it finds.

stations.name: Firewalls
teaches: A firewall controls the traffic entering and leaving a network.
It checks packets against a set of rules and blocks anything not allowed.
It can block suspicious ports, addresses and programs.
Firewalls can be hardware, software, or both.

stations.name: User access levels
teaches: Each user only gets access to what they need for their role.
Students, teachers and network managers have different rights.
If an account is compromised, the damage is limited to that user's access.

stations.name: Monitoring and policies
teaches: Network forensics means watching network traffic to detect intrusions and collect evidence.
An acceptable use policy is the set of rules a user signs up to before being allowed on the network.
Logs record who did what and when.

stations.name: Which defence?
teaches: Match the defence to the threat: anti-malware for malware, firewalls for unwanted traffic.
Access levels limit the damage when an account is compromised.
Penetration testing finds the gaps before attackers do.

outcomeText.ns-l10-o1: know how passwords, encryption and physical security help against cyberattack
outcomeText.ns-l10-o2: be able to choose suitable protections for a given threat

stations.name: Passwords
teaches: Long passwords, ideally passphrases, with a mix of characters.
Different password for every account, never shared or written down.
Backed up by lockouts and two-factor authentication.

stations.name: Encryption
teaches: Scrambles data so it can't be understood without the key.
Protects data in transit (HTTPS, WPA2, VPN) and at rest (encrypted drives).
It doesn't stop data being stolen: it makes stolen data useless.

stations.name: Physical security
teaches: Locked doors, server cabinets and equipment cages.
Keycards, visitor passes, CCTV and staffed reception desks.
Locking screens, shredding printouts and secure disposal of old drives.

stations.name: Backups and updates
teaches: Regular backups mean ransomware doesn't have to be paid.
Keep at least one backup disconnected or off-site.
Patching software closes the weaknesses worms and attackers use.

stations.name: Match the defence
teaches: Each threat has defences that work best against it.
Most real protection comes from combining several.
Your task: place each protection with the threat it stops.

stations.name: Layers of defence
teaches: No single protection stops everything, and any one can fail.
Layering means an attacker has to beat several defences in a row.
Technology, people and physical measures all matter.

outcomeText.nw-l01-o1: know what is meant by a standalone computer
outcomeText.nw-l01-o2: know the different types of network: LAN and WAN

stations.name: Standalone computer
teaches: A computer that is not connected to any other computer or network.
Its files, software and hardware can only be used on that one machine.

stations.name: Sharing a file
teaches: Without a network, files must be copied onto removable media, such as a USB stick.
The stick is then carried to the other computer and copied again.

stations.name: Printing
teaches: Each standalone computer needs its own printer, plugged in directly.
A room of 30 standalone computers could need 30 printers.

stations.name: Updates and backups
teaches: Software must be installed and updated on every computer separately.
Each computer has to be backed up on its own, which is easy to forget.

stations.name: Local area network (LAN)
teaches: Covers a small geographical area, such as one building or one school site.
The organisation owns and manages all of the hardware.
Devices connect with cables or Wi-Fi.

stations.name: Sharing resources
teaches: Files saved on a file server can be opened from any computer.
One printer can be shared by a whole room.
You can log on at any computer and see your own files.

stations.name: Advantages
teaches: Share files and hardware, such as printers.
Install software and updates on every computer from one place.
Back up everyone's data centrally.
Communicate using email and messaging.

stations.name: Disadvantages
teaches: Viruses and malware can spread from one computer to many.
Servers, switches and cabling are expensive.
A network manager is needed to run it.
If the file server fails, nobody can reach their files.

stations.name: Wide area network (WAN)
teaches: Covers a large geographical area: across towns, countries or the whole world.
Connects LANs together.
The internet is the biggest WAN.

stations.name: Who owns the connections?
teaches: WAN links are usually owned by telecoms companies. Organisations rent (lease) them.
Links include fibre optic cables (some under the sea), phone lines and satellites.

outcomeText.nw-l02-o1: understand what factors can affect the performance of a network
outcomeText.nw-l02-o2: be able to explain how each factor affects network speed

outcomeText.nw-l03-o1: know what a client-server model is
outcomeText.nw-l03-o2: know what a peer-to-peer model is
outcomeText.nw-l03-o3: understand the different roles computers have in each model

stations.name: Client-server model
teaches: A central server provides services such as files, logins, email or web pages.
Clients request services from the server, and the server responds.
Used by most schools and businesses.

stations.name: Peer-to-peer model
teaches: There is no central server: every computer is an equal peer.
Peers share files and resources directly with each other.
Each user looks after their own files, security and backups.

stations.name: Client-server: pros and cons
teaches: Easier to manage security, backups and software updates from one place.
Expensive to set up, and needs IT specialists to maintain it.
The server is a single point of failure.

stations.name: Peer-to-peer: pros and cons
teaches: Cheaper and easier to set up: no expensive server is needed.
No dependency on a single machine.
Less secure, harder to keep files organised, and users must do their own backups.

stations.name: Who's who?
teaches: Servers provide services and resources.
Clients request them.
Peers do both, as equals.

stations.name: How torrents work
teaches: A big file is split into many small pieces.
Your computer downloads different pieces from lots of other users at once, and uploads pieces to others.
The more people sharing, the faster it can be.

outcomeText.nw-l04-o1: know the hardware needed to connect a LAN
outcomeText.nw-l04-o2: understand the purpose of each piece of hardware and the jobs it does

stations.name: Switch
teaches: Connects devices together on a LAN.
Receives data and forwards it only to the device it is meant for, using MAC addresses.
Has many ports: one for each wired device.

stations.name: UTP cable
teaches: Copper wires twisted in pairs. The twist reduces interference.
Cat5e and Cat6 are common types. Cheap, flexible and easy to fit with an RJ45 plug.
Each cable run works up to about 100 m.

stations.name: Router
teaches: Connects different networks together, such as the school LAN and the internet.
Sends packets towards their destination using IP addresses.
Sits at the edge of the LAN.

stations.name: Fibre optic cable
teaches: Sends data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass.
Very high bandwidth over long distances (many kilometres).
Not affected by electrical interference, but costs more and is harder to install.

stations.name: Network interface card
teaches: Hardware that lets a device connect to a network.
Can be wired (Ethernet port) or wireless (built-in antenna).
Every NIC has a unique MAC address, set when it is made.

outcomeText.nw-l05-o1: understand what the internet actually is
outcomeText.nw-l05-o2: understand the terms Domain Name Service and domain name server
outcomeText.nw-l05-o3: understand what is meant by hosting and the cloud
outcomeText.nw-l05-o4: understand what is meant by the terms web server and client

stations.name: What is the internet?
teaches: A worldwide collection of computer networks: the biggest WAN.
Networks are joined by routers and linked by cables, including undersea fibre.
The World Wide Web is a service that uses the internet; it isn't the internet itself.

stations.name: Domain Name Service (DNS)
teaches: People use domain names like www.google.com; computers use IP addresses.
DNS turns a domain name into the matching IP address.
DNS is made up of many domain name servers, not just one.

stations.name: Hosting
teaches: Hosting means storing websites, files or services on a server so others can reach them over the internet.
Hosting companies run data centres full of servers and rent out space.

stations.name: The cloud
teaches: Storage, software and services on remote servers, accessed over the internet.
Examples: Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive.
You can reach your files from any device, anywhere with a connection.

stations.name: Web servers and clients
teaches: A web server stores web pages and sends them to clients when they are requested.
A client, such as the browser on your phone, requests a page and displays it.

stations.name: File servers
teaches: A file server stores files centrally for everyone on a network.
A desktop PC is a client: it requests a file, and the file server sends it.

outcomeText.nw-l06-o1: know what a star network is
outcomeText.nw-l06-o2: know what a mesh network is
outcomeText.nw-l06-o3: understand that the internet is an example of a partial mesh network
outcomeText.nw-l06-o4: know the advantages and disadvantages of star and mesh networks

stations.name: Star topology
teaches: Every device connects to a central switch with its own cable.
All data travels through the switch, which sends it on to the device it is meant for.

stations.name: Advantages of star
teaches: If one cable fails, only that device is affected.
Easy to add a new device: just plug in one more cable.
Fast and reliable: the switch only sends data where it needs to go.

stations.name: Disadvantages of star
teaches: If the central switch fails, every device loses its connection. It is a single point of failure.
Every device needs its own cable back to the switch, so it uses a lot of cable, which costs money.

stations.name: Joining star networks
teaches: Bigger networks join several stars together by linking their switches with a cable.
Devices on different switches communicate over this link.

stations.name: Full mesh
teaches: Every device is connected directly to every other device.
Data can travel along many different routes to reach its destination.

stations.name: Mesh: pros and cons
teaches: No single point of failure: if a link fails, data is rerouted along another path.
Can handle lots of traffic, because data is spread across many routes.
Needs a lot of cable and is difficult to set up, so it is expensive.

stations.name: Partial mesh: the internet
teaches: In a partial mesh, devices connect to several others, but not to all of them.
The internet is a partial mesh: routers link to a few other routers, so there is always another route.

stations.name: Wireless mesh
teaches: Wireless access points connect to each other by Wi-Fi. Each one must be in range of at least one other.
Only one WAP needs a cable. Coverage is easy to extend, but data slows down as it hops between WAPs.

outcomeText.nw-l07-o1: know which lessons I am secure on and which I need to revise
outcomeText.nw-l07-o2: have completed any outstanding work from lessons 1 to 6
outcomeText.nw-l07-o3: be ready for my mid-topic test next lesson

outcomeText.nw-l09-o1: understand that Ethernet is a wired method of connection
outcomeText.nw-l09-o2: understand that Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are wireless methods of connection
outcomeText.nw-l09-o3: understand the benefits and drawbacks of wired versus wireless connections
outcomeText.nw-l09-o4: be able to recommend a connection type for a specified scenario

stations.name: Ethernet
teaches: A wired standard for connecting devices on a LAN.
Data is sent in frames containing source and destination addresses.
Uses twisted pair or fibre optic cable, usually into a switch.

stations.name: Wi-Fi
teaches: A wireless connection using radio waves, through a wireless access point.
Range of around 100 metres, less indoors.
High bandwidth, but uses more power than Bluetooth.

stations.name: Bluetooth
teaches: A short-range wireless connection directly between two devices.
Range of around 10 metres.
Low bandwidth and low power consumption.

stations.name: Wi-Fi vs Bluetooth
teaches: Complete the table on your worksheet for range, bandwidth and power consumption.

stations.name: Wired vs wireless
teaches: Wired: faster, more reliable and easier to secure, but needs lots of cabling.
Wireless: access from anywhere in range and less disruptive to set up, but slower, less secure, and blocked by walls.

stations.name: Recommend a connection
teaches: Think about speed, reliability, security, range, power use and how easy it is to set up.
Always justify your choice with the scenario.

outcomeText.nw-l10-o1: know the basics of how cryptography can work with a simple key
outcomeText.nw-l10-o2: know how wireless devices authenticate each other before communicating data
outcomeText.nw-l10-o3: understand the difference between private and public keys
outcomeText.nw-l10-o4: understand why private keys are never shared

stations.name: Why encrypt?
teaches: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
Wi-Fi signals travel through the air, so anyone in range could intercept them.
Encrypted data is useless to anyone without the key.

stations.name: ROT13 and the Romans
teaches: A substitution cipher replaces each letter with another one, using a rule or key.
ROT13 moves each letter 13 places: A becomes N. Doing it twice gives the original back.
Julius Caesar used a shift cipher to send secret messages.

stations.name: Keys
teaches: The key is the secret used to encrypt and decrypt a message.
Without the key, the message is very hard to work out.
If a key is sent with the message it could be intercepted, so master keys are known but never sent.

stations.name: Public and private keys
teaches: A public key can be shared with anyone; it's used to encrypt messages sent to you.
Only your matching private key can decrypt them.
So the private key is never shared with anyone.

stations.name: The WPA2 handshake
teaches: Before any data is sent, the device and the access point check each other.
Both work out the same master key from the Wi-Fi password.
They swap random numbers to calculate a temporary key, without ever sending the key itself.

stations.name: Staying safe on Wi-Fi
teaches: Use networks protected with WPA2 or WPA3.
Open networks with no password send data without Wi-Fi encryption.
A strong Wi-Fi password matters, because the master key is made from it.

outcomeText.nw-l11-o1: understand the uses of MAC and IP addressing
outcomeText.nw-l11-o2: understand the difference between IPv4 and IPv6

stations.name: MAC addresses
teaches: Media Access Control address: a unique address given to every network interface card when it is made.
48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits in pairs.
Used by switches to send frames to the right device on a LAN.

stations.name: IP addresses
teaches: Internet Protocol address: identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
Given by the network, so it can change when a device moves to another network.
Used by routers to send packets across networks.

stations.name: IPv4
teaches: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots.
Part of the address identifies the network; the rest identifies the device (node).
There are about 4.3 billion possible addresses: not enough for every device today.

stations.name: IPv6
teaches: 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.
Created because IPv4 addresses were running out.
Allows about 340 undecillion (3.4 × 10³⁸) addresses.

stations.name: LAN or WAN addressing?
teaches: Within a LAN, switches use MAC addresses to deliver frames.
Between networks, routers use IP addresses to route packets.
Every device has both.

stations.name: Network and device parts
teaches: In 192.168.1.20, the first part (192.168.1) identifies the network.
The last part (20) identifies the device, or node, on that network.
Devices on the same network share the network part.

outcomeText.nw-l12-o1: understand the need for standards in computing
outcomeText.nw-l12-o2: understand the seven common protocols and what they are used for

stations.name: Standards
teaches: Agreed rules and specifications so hardware and software from different makers work together.
Examples: USB, Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Ethernet and HTML.
Without standards, devices couldn't talk to each other.

stations.name: Protocols
teaches: A protocol is a set of rules that governs how devices communicate on a network.
It covers the format of data, addressing and how errors are handled.
Different protocols do different jobs.

stations.name: Web protocols
teaches: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): a client-server way of requesting and delivering HTML files.
HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): adds encryption and authentication.
Look for the padlock in your browser.

stations.name: Email protocols
teaches: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email to a mail server.
POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves email from a mail server.
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) retrieves email and manages it on the server, so it syncs across devices.

stations.name: FTP
teaches: File Transfer Protocol: sends files between computers.
Often used to upload web pages and their files to a web server for hosting.

stations.name: TCP/IP
teaches: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): splits data into packets and makes sure they all arrive, error-free and in order.
IP (Internet Protocol): routes packets across a wide area network using IP addresses.
They work together as TCP/IP.

stations.name: Why layers?
teaches: Networking is a complex job, so it's divided into smaller, simpler tasks called layers.
Each layer has a defined responsibility.
Each layer provides a service to the layer above it.

stations.name: The parcel model
teaches: A parcel goes in a box, the box goes in a sack, the sack goes in a van.
Swap the van for a train and the parcel inside doesn't change at all.
Each stage only has to deal with the stage next to it.

stations.name: Advantages of layering
teaches: Easier to develop and troubleshoot: you can work on one layer at a time.
Layers can be changed or upgraded independently.
Different companies can make products for different layers that still work together.

stations.name: The four layers
teaches: Application: the programs you use, e.g. HTTP, SMTP, FTP.
Transport: TCP makes sure data arrives reliably.
Internet: IP routes packets.  Link: the physical connection, e.g. Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

stations.name: Sending an email
teaches: Your email app uses SMTP (application layer).
TCP makes sure it all arrives (transport layer).
IP routes it to the mail server (internet layer), over Wi-Fi (link layer).

stations.name: Layers in action
teaches: Loading a web page: HTTP (or HTTPS), then TCP, then IP, then Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
Each layer adds its own information, like putting a letter in an envelope.
The receiver unwraps the layers in reverse.

outcomeText.nw-l14-o1: know which lessons I am secure on and which to revise
outcomeText.nw-l14-o2: be ready for the end-of-unit assessment

stations.name: Lesson 9: Modes of connection
teaches: Ethernet is wired: fast, reliable and secure, but needs cabling.
Wi-Fi is wireless, about 100 m range, high bandwidth.
Bluetooth: about 10 m, low bandwidth, low power.

stations.name: Lesson 10: Wi-Fi encryption
teaches: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
A public key is shared; a private key is never shared.
WPA2 authenticates devices without sending the key.

stations.name: Lesson 11: IP and MAC addressing
teaches: MAC: 48 bits, hexadecimal pairs, set when the NIC is made; used in a LAN.
IPv4: 32 bits, four numbers 0 to 255.
IPv6: 128 bits, hexadecimal groups; needed because IPv4 ran out.

stations.name: Lesson 12: Standards and protocols
teaches: Standards let hardware and software from different makers work together.
A protocol is a set of rules for communication.
HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP, TCP/IP.
