stations.name: Lesson 13: Layers
teaches: Networking is divided into layers, each with a defined job.
Each layer provides a service to the layer above.
A layer can be changed without affecting the others.

stations.name: Exam technique
teaches: State: give a short fact. Describe: give the key features. Explain: say how or why, using 'because'.
Match your answer to the marks: one point per mark.
Use the key terms from this unit.

outcomeText.pf-l01-o1: know what variables and constants are, and how a value is assigned to each
outcomeText.pf-l01-o2: understand how input and output move data in and out of a program
outcomeText.pf-l01-o3: know what sequence, selection and iteration each do to the order a program runs in

stations.name: Variables and assignment
teaches: A variable is a named location in memory holding a value that can change while the program runs.
Assignment uses a single equals sign: the value on the right is stored in the variable on the left.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language, score = score + 10 reads the old value, adds ten, then stores the result back.

stations.name: Constants
teaches: A constant is a named value that is set when the program is written and cannot change while it runs.
Constants make a program easier to read, and a value used many times can be changed in one place.
A VAT rate or the number of lives a player starts with are good constants.

stations.name: Input and output
teaches: Input brings data into a program, usually from the keyboard. Output sends data out, usually to the screen.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language input() and print() do this work.
input() always returns a string, so a number must be cast before it is used in arithmetic.

stations.name: Sequence
teaches: Sequence means the statements are carried out one after another, in the order they are written.
Change the order and you usually change the result.
A variable must be given a value before any line that uses it.

stations.name: Selection
teaches: Selection chooses which statements to run by testing a condition that is either True or False.
if ... then runs a block only when the condition is True; else runs when it is False; elseif tests a further condition.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language the block ends with endif.

stations.name: Iteration
teaches: Iteration repeats a set of statements. A count-controlled loop repeats a known number of times.
A condition-controlled loop repeats while a condition stays True, so the number of repeats is not known in advance.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language a count-controlled loop uses for and next, and a condition-controlled loop uses while and endwhile.

outcomeText.pf-l02-o1: know the data types integer, real, Boolean, character and string
outcomeText.pf-l02-o2: understand why casting is needed and how a value is cast from one type to another
outcomeText.pf-l02-o3: know how the arithmetic, comparison and Boolean operators are used

stations.name: Data types
teaches: An integer is a whole number, positive or negative, with no decimal part. A real holds a number with a decimal part.
A Boolean holds only True or False.
A character is one single symbol; a string is a sequence of characters, and may be empty.

stations.name: Casting
teaches: Casting converts a value from one data type to another.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language int() casts to an integer, float() to a real, str() to a string and bool() to a Boolean.
Casting is needed because input() always returns a string, and strings cannot be used in arithmetic.

stations.name: Arithmetic operators
teaches: The arithmetic operators are + to add, - to subtract, * to multiply and / to divide.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language the exponent operator is ^, so 3 ^ 2 means 3 to the power 2, which is 9.
The usual order of operations applies: brackets, then exponents, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.

stations.name: MOD and DIV
teaches: DIV gives the whole number part of a division and throws the remainder away, so 17 DIV 5 is 3.
MOD gives the remainder left after a whole number division, so 17 MOD 5 is 2.
MOD 2 is a quick test for an even number, because an even number always leaves a remainder of 0.

stations.name: Comparison and Boolean operators
teaches: The comparison operators are ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=, and each one gives True or False.
AND is True only when both conditions are True. OR is True when at least one condition is True.
NOT reverses a condition, so NOT True gives False.

stations.name: String manipulation
teaches: The length of a string is the number of characters in it, counting spaces.
A substring is a part of a string, taken from a given position. Concatenation joins strings together using +.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language name.length, name.substring(0, 3), name.upper and name.lower do this work, and ASC() and CHR() convert between a character and its ASCII code.

outcomeText.pf-l03-o1: know why a program needs to store data in a file
outcomeText.pf-l03-o2: understand how a file is opened, read from, written to and closed
outcomeText.pf-l03-o3: know the difference between writing to a file and appending to it

stations.name: Why files
teaches: Data held in variables is lost as soon as the program stops, because variables are held in RAM.
Writing data to a file stores it on secondary storage, so it is still there the next time the program runs.
Files also let the output of one program become the input of another.

stations.name: Opening a file
teaches: A file must be opened before a program can read from it or write to it.
Opening a file gives the program a handle: a name it uses to refer to that file from then on.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language, newFile("scores.txt") creates a new file and openRead("scores.txt") opens one that already exists.

stations.name: Reading a file
teaches: Reading copies data from the file into the program, usually one line at a time.
A condition-controlled loop reads line by line until the end of the file is reached.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language, readLine() gets the next line and endOfFile() becomes True when there are no lines left.

stations.name: Writing to a file
teaches: Writing copies data out of the program and into the file, so it is saved on secondary storage.
In Python 3, open("scores.txt", "w") opens a file for writing and deletes anything that was already in it.
Data written to a file is not safe until the file has been closed.

stations.name: Appending
teaches: Appending adds new data to the end of a file and keeps everything that was already there.
In Python 3, open("log.txt", "a") opens a file in append mode.
Appending suits a log or a high score table, where the old records must not be lost.

stations.name: Closing the file
teaches: Closing a file tells the operating system that the program has finished with it.
Data written to a file may still be waiting in a buffer in memory, and closing the file makes sure it reaches the disk.
A file left open can stop other programs using it, and wastes memory.

outcomeText.pf-l04-o1: know what is meant by a record, a field and a table of records
outcomeText.pf-l04-o2: understand how SELECT, FROM and WHERE are used to search for data
outcomeText.pf-l04-o3: know how AND, OR, NOT and LIKE narrow a search down

stations.name: What is a record
teaches: A record is one row of related data about a single thing, such as one packet of seed in the library.
The separate pieces of data inside a record are called fields, and each field has its own name.
A table is a set of records that all have exactly the same fields.

stations.name: Fields and data types
teaches: Every field is given a data type, and only data of that type may be stored in it.
SeedID and PacketsLeft hold whole numbers, so they are integers. Name and Family hold characters, so they hold text.
Fields in the same record can be different data types, which is why a record is more useful than an array.

stations.name: SELECT and FROM
teaches: SQL, the structured query language, is used to search a table of records.
SELECT lists the fields you want back. FROM names the table they are taken from.
SELECT * means every field in the record, and a query with no condition returns every record in the table.

stations.name: WHERE
teaches: WHERE sets a condition, and only records where that condition is True are returned.
Conditions use =, <>, <, >, <= and >=. A piece of text is written inside single quotes.
In this table,  SELECT Name FROM Seeds WHERE Family = 'Legume';  returns Runner Bean and Sweet Pea.

stations.name: Boolean operators
teaches: AND returns a record only when both of its conditions are True.
OR returns a record when at least one of its conditions is True.
NOT reverses a condition, so  NOT Family = 'Legume'  returns every record that is not a legume.

stations.name: LIKE and wildcards
teaches: LIKE searches a text field for a pattern instead of an exact match.
The % wildcard stands for any number of characters, including none. The _ wildcard stands for exactly one character.
So  WHERE Name LIKE 'S%'  means the name must begin with S and may be followed by anything.

outcomeText.pf-l05-o1: know how one- and two-dimensional arrays are declared, read and changed
outcomeText.pf-l05-o2: understand why arrays are zero-indexed and how a loop iterates over one
outcomeText.pf-l05-o3: know the difference between a procedure and a function, and between local and global variables

stations.name: One-dimensional arrays
teaches: An array stores many values of the same data type under a single name, instead of a separate variable for each one.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language,  array crate[5]  declares an array with five elements.
An array is given its size when it is declared and keeps it; a list in Python can grow and shrink as the program runs.

stations.name: Index positions
teaches: Each element has an index, which is its position in the array. OCR arrays begin at index 0, which is called zero-indexing.
So the first element of  array crate[5]  is crate[0] and the last is crate[4]. Asking for crate[5] goes past the end and causes an error.
An element is changed by naming its index:  crate[2] = 7  replaces whatever was already in position 2. A count-controlled loop iterates over the whole array.

stations.name: Two-dimensional arrays
teaches: A two-dimensional array is a table of values with rows and columns. In the OCR Exam Reference Language,  array bay[3,4]  declares 3 rows of 4.
An element needs two indices, the row first and then the column, so bay[0,0] is the top left corner.
Two nested loops iterate over it: the outer loop moves down the rows and the inner loop across the columns.

stations.name: Procedures and functions
teaches: A sub-program is a named block of code that the main program can call, as many times as it needs, without the code being written out again.
A procedure carries out a task but returns no value. In the OCR Exam Reference Language it runs from procedure to endprocedure.
A function always returns a value to the line that called it, using return, and runs from function to endfunction.

stations.name: Parameters and returns
teaches: A parameter is a variable in the sub-program's definition that receives a value when the sub-program is called.
Parameters let the same sub-program work on different data every time, so it does not have to be rewritten.
return sends one value back to the calling line and ends the function straight away.

stations.name: Local and global
teaches: A local variable is declared inside a sub-program and only exists while that sub-program is running. Nothing outside it can see the variable.
A global variable can be used anywhere in the program. In the OCR Exam Reference Language it is declared with the keyword global.
Local variables are safer, because two sub-programs can use the same name without clashing and the memory is freed when the sub-program ends.

outcomeText.pf-l06-o1: know what random numbers are used for in a program
outcomeText.pf-l06-o2: understand how a random whole number is generated within a given range
outcomeText.pf-l06-o3: know that a computer produces pseudo-random numbers from an algorithm and a seed

stations.name: Why random numbers
teaches: A random number lets a program behave differently each time it runs, so the result cannot be predicted.
Games use them for dice rolls, card shuffles and where an enemy appears.
Simulations, random sampling, shuffling a list and generating a password all need them too.

stations.name: Generating a random number
teaches: In the OCR Exam Reference Language, random(1, 6) returns a random whole number from 1 to 6, and both end points are included.
The value returned is normally stored in a variable, so the program can use that one number more than once.
Calling the function a second time gives a fresh number, which may or may not be the same as the first.

stations.name: Choosing the range
teaches: The two values passed to the function set the lowest and the highest number that can be returned.
In Python 3, random.randint(1, 6) can return 6, but random.randrange(1, 6) stops at 5.
An array of five elements is indexed 0 to 4, so a random index must come from that range and no wider.

stations.name: Pseudo-random
teaches: A computer cannot be truly random: it works each number out with an algorithm, so the numbers are called pseudo-random.
The algorithm starts from a value called the seed, and the same seed always produces the same sequence of numbers.
Most languages take the seed from the computer's clock, so the sequence is different each time the program runs.

stations.name: Random in a loop
teaches: A new number is generated every time the function is called, so a loop can produce a whole set of them.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language a count-controlled loop suits a known number of values, such as ten dice rolls.
Each call is independent of the last, so the same value can come up twice in a row.

stations.name: Using randomness well
teaches: A simulation uses random numbers to model something unpredictable, such as traffic or the weather, so it can be run many times.
Random sampling picks members of a group at random, so the sample is fair and not chosen on purpose.
A shuffle puts a list into a random order, and a password generator picks random characters.

outcomeText.pf-l07-o1: know the whole of topic 2.2 well enough to answer without notes
outcomeText.pf-l07-o2: understand the mistakes that most often lose marks in programming questions
outcomeText.pf-l07-o3: know which lessons are secure and which still need revision before the test

stations.name: Constructs recap
teaches: A single equals sign assigns a value to a variable; a double equals sign compares two values and gives True or False.
Selection makes a choice once. Iteration goes back and repeats.
A condition-controlled loop must change the variable in its condition somewhere inside the loop, or it never ends.

stations.name: Types and operators recap
teaches: In the OCR Exam Reference Language, + joins two strings but adds two numbers, so "7" + "2" gives the string 72 while 7 + 2 gives 9.
input() always returns a string, so a number must be cast before any arithmetic is done with it.
DIV gives how many whole times one number goes into another, and MOD gives the remainder left over.

stations.name: File handling recap
teaches: In Python 3, mode "w" wipes whatever was in the file, and mode "a" adds to the end and keeps what was already there.
In the OCR Exam Reference Language a read loop calls readLine() inside the loop and stops when endOfFile() becomes True.
A file must be closed, or the last data written may never leave the buffer in memory.

stations.name: Records and SQL recap
teaches: SELECT chooses the fields, FROM chooses the table and WHERE chooses the records.
Text in a WHERE condition goes inside single quotes, and a pattern with a wildcard needs LIKE rather than =.
AND needs both of its conditions to be True, so it returns the same number of records as OR or fewer.

stations.name: Arrays and sub-programs recap
teaches: An array of n elements is indexed 0 to n - 1, so the last index is always one less than the size.
A function returns a value to the line that called it, and a procedure does not.
A local variable only exists inside its own sub-program, so no other part of the program can read it.

stations.name: Randomness recap
teaches: In the OCR Exam Reference Language, random(1, 6) includes both 1 and 6.
A computer produces pseudo-random numbers with an algorithm and a seed, so the same seed gives the same sequence.
A random index must stay inside the array, so an array of six elements needs a number from 0 to 5.

outcomeText.pl-l01-o2: Explain why high-level source needs translation.
outcomeText.pl-l01-o3: Justify language choices using project requirements.

stations.name: High-level languages
teaches: Use readable words and familiar operations to express a solution.
Hide many details of how the processor works.
Usually easier to write, understand and maintain.

stations.name: Low-level languages
teaches: Close to the instructions and hardware of a processor.
Machine code and assembly are low-level languages.
Offer detailed control, but are harder to write and maintain.

stations.name: Machine code
teaches: Binary instructions that a compatible CPU can execute.
Each processor family has its own instruction set.
Difficult for people to read, write and check directly.

stations.name: The need for translation
teaches: Programmers write source code to express instructions.
A CPU cannot execute high-level source directly.
A translator enables the source program to be executed.

stations.name: Moving between devices
teaches: High-level source is often more portable between systems.
A suitable translator or runtime must be available.
Low-level code may need rewriting for another instruction set.

stations.name: Choosing the right level
teaches: Match the language to the requirements of the project.
High-level code can reduce development and maintenance effort.
Low-level code can provide fine control of speed and memory use.

outcomeText.pl-l02-o1: Compare development effort at different language levels.
outcomeText.pl-l02-o3: Justify language choices using project requirements.

stations.name: Reading and changing code
teaches: High-level code uses readable words and structures.
Readable code is usually easier to understand and change.
Low-level code requires more knowledge of the processor.

stations.name: Development time
teaches: High-level operations can express a task in fewer instructions.
Low-level code often needs more detailed instructions.
More detailed code can take longer to write and check.

stations.name: Moving to another system
teaches: High-level source is usually more portable.
The new system needs a suitable translator.
Low-level code is tied more closely to a processor.

stations.name: Control of hardware
teaches: Low-level code closely matches processor operations.
It allows detailed control of hardware and memory use.
This control comes with greater development effort.

stations.name: Speed and memory
teaches: Low-level code can be carefully tuned for a processor.
This can help control execution speed and memory use.
High-level code usually makes development easier.

stations.name: A justified recommendation
teaches: Identify the main requirement in the project.
Choose the language level that addresses it.
Explain both the benefit and a relevant drawback.

outcomeText.pl-l03-o2: Compare how compilers and interpreters work.
outcomeText.pl-l03-o3: Justify a translator choice using the task requirements.

stations.name: Why translate?
teaches: Source code expresses a program in a human-readable language.
A CPU executes compatible machine instructions.
A translator connects the source language to execution.

stations.name: The compiler route
teaches: A compiler processes the source program before execution.
It reports translation errors it finds.
A successful build can produce code that is run later.

stations.name: The interpreter route
teaches: An interpreter processes source instructions as they execute.
It typically stops when it encounters an error it cannot handle.
The usual GCSE model has no separate standalone executable.

stations.name: Error reporting
teaches: A compiler reports errors found during translation.
An interpreter stops at an error as it processes the source.
Immediate feedback can help the programmer locate a problem.

stations.name: Running and distributing
teaches: Compilation takes time before the first run.
Compiled code runs without repeating source translation.
Interpreted source needs translation each time it runs.

stations.name: Choosing a route
teaches: Frequent edits can favour an interpreter during development.
Repeated distribution can favour a compiled build.
Give a reason linked to the stated requirement.

outcomeText.pl-l04-o1: Identify the four main IDE facilities.
outcomeText.pl-l04-o2: Explain how each facility supports programming.
outcomeText.pl-l04-o3: Use editing, diagnostics and execution tools in an IDE.

stations.name: Tools in one place
teaches: An IDE combines programming facilities in one application.
Editors and diagnostics help create and correct source.
Translators and a run-time environment help execute it.

stations.name: Writing source code
teaches: Syntax highlighting uses colour to distinguish code elements.
Auto-completion suggests names or code as you type.
Indentation tools help present blocks clearly.

stations.name: The run-time environment
teaches: A run-time environment lets a programmer execute a program.
Input and output can be handled during the run.
The programmer can observe the program’s behaviour.

stations.name: Diagnostic messages
teaches: Diagnostics identify detected problems in the code.
A message can include a line number and an error description.
Read the surrounding code before deciding on a repair.

stations.name: Translators in an IDE
teaches: An IDE can use a compiler or an interpreter.
The translator processes the program’s source instructions.
Translation and execution have different roles.

stations.name: Using your class IDE
teaches: Open the IDE your teacher uses for programming.
Use its editor, Run control and output area.
Read a diagnostic message and correct its cause.

outcomeText.pl-l05-o1: Recall language levels and translator behaviour.
outcomeText.pl-l05-o2: Select IDE tools for specific problems.
outcomeText.pl-l05-o3: Write explanations linked to the needs of a scenario.

stations.name: Language decisions
teaches: High-level languages hide many hardware details.
Low-level languages expose processor operations.
The project requirements should guide the choice.

stations.name: Source and execution
teaches: Programmers write source code.
High-level source needs translation before the CPU can execute its instructions.
A CPU executes compatible machine code.

stations.name: Translator choices
teaches: Compilers process source before the translated program runs.
Interpreters process source during execution.
Compiled code can run again without source translation.

stations.name: Editing and diagnostics
teaches: An editor lets a programmer write and change source.
Highlighting helps distinguish code elements.
Diagnostics describe detected problems.

stations.name: Translation and running
teaches: An IDE can call a compiler or interpreter.
The run-time environment executes the program.
Input and output let the programmer interact with a run.

stations.name: Writing an explanation
teaches: Read the programmer’s requirement.
Name a relevant language characteristic or IDE facility.
Explain how it helps in that situation.

outcomeText.pr-l01-o1: know how to print lines of output in the order a task asks for
outcomeText.pr-l01-o2: know how to hold a value in a variable or a constant, and how to read one with input()
outcomeText.pr-l01-o3: understand why a value that has been typed in must be cast before it can be calculated with

stations.name: Printing output
teaches: print() puts one value on the screen and then moves down to the next line.
Text to be shown exactly as written goes inside quotation marks, and one print() gives one line of output.
Common mistake: leaving the quotation marks off, so Python hunts for a variable with that name instead.

stations.name: Variables
teaches: A variable is a named box in memory holding one value, and the name always goes on the left of the equals sign.
A constant is a value the program never changes once it is set, and its name is written in capitals.
Common mistake: a second assignment replaces the value, it does not add to it.

stations.name: Reading input
teaches: input() stops the program, waits for a line to be typed and hands that line back.
Store what comes back in a variable, or the value the user typed is thrown away.
Common mistake: reading two answers into the same variable, so the first one is lost.

stations.name: Numbers and text
teaches: Integers count whole things, floats hold decimals, strings hold text and booleans hold True or False.
+ adds two numbers but joins two strings end to end, so the data type decides what + means.
Common mistake: joining a number to a string with +, which Python refuses to do.

stations.name: Casting
teaches: Casting changes a value from one data type into another.
int() and float() turn text into a number, and str() turns a number into text.
Common mistake: adding to what input() handed back without casting it first, which joins the digits on the end instead.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: A whole program reads its values, works something out and then prints the lines it was asked for.
Decide the data type each value needs before you write a single line.
Common mistake: printing the lines in a different order from the one the task asked for.

stations.name: Final challenge: name the data type

outcomeText.pr-l02-o1: know which arithmetic operator each kind of calculation needs
outcomeText.pr-l02-o2: understand the difference between /, // and % and what each one hands back
outcomeText.pr-l02-o3: know how to round a result, and how to draw a random number from a seed

stations.name: The four operations
teaches: + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies and / divides.
/ always gives a float, so 10 / 2 shows as 5.0 rather than 5.
Common mistake: writing 2n for two lots of n, when Python needs 2 * n.

stations.name: Whole number division
teaches: // divides and throws the remainder away, giving a whole number.
% gives only the remainder, and is called the modulus.
Common mistake: using / when the answer must be whole, which leaves a .0 on the end.

stations.name: Powers and roots
teaches: ** raises a number to a power, so 5 ** 2 is 25 and 5 ** 3 is 125.
A square root is the power of 0.5, or math.sqrt() once math has been imported.
Common mistake: writing 5 ^ 2, which does something else entirely in Python.

stations.name: Rounding
teaches: round(x) gives the nearest whole number, and round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places.
abs() removes the sign, so a difference can be reported without saying which way.
Common mistake: rounding early, then carrying the rounded value into the next calculation.

stations.name: Random numbers
teaches: import random first, then random.randint(a, b) gives a whole number from a to b, both included.
random.seed(n) makes the same sequence come out every time, so an answer can be marked.
Common mistake: calling randint again instead of storing the number you have already drawn.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Work out the order of a calculation before you type it: brackets, powers, then * / // %, then + -.
Store a part-finished answer in a named variable to keep a long calculation readable.
Common mistake: leaving brackets out, so Python works the sum out in a different order from the one you meant.

outcomeText.pr-l03-o1: know how to write a condition using the comparison operators
outcomeText.pr-l03-o2: understand how if, elif and else choose between several outcomes
outcomeText.pr-l03-o3: know how to join two conditions together with and, or and not

stations.name: Comparing values
teaches: A comparison gives a boolean back: either True or False.
The comparison operators are ==, !=, >, <, >= and <=.
Common mistake: comparing with one =, when one = stores a value and two compare them.

stations.name: if and else
teaches: if runs the indented block below it only when its condition is True.
else catches every other case, and needs no condition of its own.
Common mistake: missing the colon, or not indenting the block underneath it.

stations.name: elif
teaches: elif adds another condition, which is only tested if the ones above it were False.
Python stops at the first branch that is True and skips everything below.
Common mistake: putting a wide band first, so it catches everything and the later branches never run.

stations.name: AND, OR and NOT
teaches: and is True only when both sides are, and or is True when at least one side is.
not flips a condition over, so not found is True whenever found is False.
Common mistake: writing n == 3 or 7, which Python reads as something quite different.

stations.name: Decisions inside decisions
teaches: A decision can sit inside another, and the inner one is only reached if the outer was True.
Each level of nesting is indented one more step in than the one above.
Common mistake: nesting where a single and would have said the same thing far more clearly.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Work the boundaries out first, then write the bands in the order the rules apply.
Test on the edge of every band, because that is exactly where conditions go wrong.
Common mistake: using > where the rule says 'or more', which loses the boundary value.

outcomeText.pr-l04-o1: know how to write a for loop that repeats a block a set number of times
outcomeText.pr-l04-o2: understand how range() decides which values the loop counter takes
outcomeText.pr-l04-o3: know how to build a running total inside a loop, and how to put one loop inside another

stations.name: Repeating a line
teaches: for i in range(4): runs the indented block below it four times.
Count-controlled iteration is used when the number of repeats is known in advance.
Common mistake: leaving the line to repeat outside the loop, so it only runs once.

stations.name: Using the counter
teaches: The loop variable holds the count on each pass, so you can print it or calculate with it.
range(n) counts from 0, so the values are 0 up to n - 1.
Common mistake: expecting range(5) to include 5, or to start at 1.

stations.name: Choosing the range
teaches: range(start, stop) counts from start up to but not including stop.
A third value is the step, so range(10, 0, -2) counts back down in twos.
Common mistake: forgetting stop is never reached, which quietly loses the last value.

stations.name: Running totals
teaches: A running total is set to 0 before the loop and grows inside it.
total = total + value adds this pass's value to whatever is already there.
Common mistake: setting the total back to 0 inside the loop, which loses everything counted so far.

stations.name: Loops inside loops
teaches: A nested loop runs the whole inner loop on every single pass of the outer one.
Rows and columns are the usual job: the outer loop picks the row, the inner one the column.
Common mistake: indenting the inner loop's body wrongly, so all the rows run together.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Decide what each loop counts before you write it, and name the loop variable after that.
Build the total, the count and the average from the same single pass through the data.
Common mistake: printing inside the loop when the task asks for one line at the end.

outcomeText.pr-l05-o1: know how to write a while loop and what makes it stop repeating
outcomeText.pr-l05-o2: understand how a validation loop keeps asking until the value typed in is acceptable
outcomeText.pr-l05-o3: know how a sentinel value ends a loop when the amount of data is not known in advance

stations.name: A loop with a condition
teaches: while repeats its block for as long as its condition stays True.
The condition is tested before every pass, so a while loop can run no times at all.
Common mistake: never changing the condition inside the loop, which leaves it running forever.

stations.name: Asking until it is right
teaches: A validation loop reads a value, then asks again for as long as it breaks the rules.
Read once above the loop, then read again at the bottom of it.
Common mistake: leaving the second read out, so the same bad value is tested forever.

stations.name: Sentinel values
teaches: A sentinel is an agreed value meaning 'no more data', such as -1 or the word end.
The loop keeps going until the sentinel arrives, however many values came before it.
Common mistake: counting the sentinel itself as one of the real values.

stations.name: Counting inside a while
teaches: A counter and a running total are set up before the loop and updated inside it.
The same pass can count the values and test each one against a rule.
Common mistake: updating the counter after the loop has already finished.

stations.name: Choosing for or while
teaches: Use for when the number of repeats is known before the loop starts.
Use while when it depends on the data, or on what the user chooses to type.
Common mistake: a while loop with its own counter where a for loop would be shorter and safer.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Set every total and counter up before the loop, and report them after it.
One while loop can both check what comes in and gather the figures you need.
Common mistake: reporting inside the loop, which prints a line for every value read.

outcomeText.pr-l06-o1: know how to find the length of a string and the character at a given position
outcomeText.pr-l06-o2: understand how a slice takes part of a string, and why its end position is left out
outcomeText.pr-l06-o3: know how to change case, search inside text, and move between a character and its code

stations.name: Length and position
teaches: len() gives the number of characters in a string, spaces included.
Characters are numbered from 0, so the last one sits at len() - 1.
Common mistake: asking for position len(), which is one past the end and stops the program.

stations.name: Taking part of a string
teaches: A slice takes a run of characters, so word[0:3] gives the first three.
The first number is included and the second is not, exactly like range().
Common mistake: expecting word[0:3] to give four characters rather than three.

stations.name: Upper and lower case
teaches: upper() and lower() hand back a new string and leave the original untouched.
Comparing two strings in the same case ignores how they happened to be typed.
Common mistake: calling lower() but never storing or using what it gives back.

stations.name: Searching inside text
teaches: in tests whether one string appears anywhere inside another.
find() gives the position it starts at, or -1 when it is not there at all.
Common mistake: treating find()'s 0 as 'not found', when 0 means the very start.

stations.name: Character codes
teaches: Every character is stored as a number, and ord() gives that number.
chr() goes the other way, turning a code back into its character.
Common mistake: adding 1 to the letter itself, when it is the code that has to be added to.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Build a new string one character at a time inside a loop over the original.
isalpha() and isdigit() sort the letters from the digits as you go.
Common mistake: trying to change one character in place, when a string cannot be edited.

stations.name: Final challenge: what does it give?

outcomeText.pr-l07-o1: know how to create a list and read one item out of it by its index
outcomeText.pr-l07-o2: understand how to traverse a list in order to total, count or compare its items
outcomeText.pr-l07-o3: know how to add an item onto a list and how to take one out again

stations.name: Making a list
teaches: Square brackets make a list, with the items separated by commas.
A list can start out empty and be filled by a loop as the values arrive.
Common mistake: creating the empty list inside the loop, which throws each item away again.

stations.name: Reading an item
teaches: A list is indexed from 0, so the third item sits at position 2.
len() gives how many items there are, which makes the last index len() - 1.
Common mistake: an index past the end, which stops the program with an error.

stations.name: Going through a list
teaches: for item in list: hands you each value in turn.
for i in range(len(list)): gives the positions instead, for when you need the index too.
Common mistake: printing the index when the task asked for the value, or the other way round.

stations.name: Adding and removing
teaches: append() adds one item onto the end of the list.
remove() takes out the first item with that value, and pop(i) takes out the one at position i.
Common mistake: removing items while looping over the same list, which makes the loop skip some.

stations.name: Totals and averages
teaches: Total the list in a loop, then divide by len() to get the average.
Track the largest and smallest by comparing each item against the best found so far.
Common mistake: starting the largest at 0, which fails on a list of negative numbers.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: One pass can build the total, count the items and remember where the largest one was.
Report the figures after the loop has finished, not while it is still running.
Common mistake: finding the largest value but forgetting to record the position it was found at.

stations.name: Final challenge: what does it do?

outcomeText.pr-l08-o1: know how to build a two-dimensional list as a list of lists and fill it from input
outcomeText.pr-l08-o2: understand how a row index and a column index together pick out one cell
outcomeText.pr-l08-o3: know how to write nested loops that print a grid and total any row or column of it

stations.name: A list of lists
teaches: A two-dimensional array is a list whose items are themselves lists.
Each inner list is one row, and the rows normally all hold the same number of items.
Common mistake: expecting len() on a grid to count the cells, when it counts the rows.

stations.name: Rows and columns
teaches: grid[row][col] reads one cell, with the row first and the column second.
grid[row] on its own gives back that whole row as a list.
Common mistake: swapping the two indexes over, which reads a completely different cell.

stations.name: Going through a grid
teaches: Two nested loops visit every cell: the outer picks the row, the inner the column.
Print a new line after the inner loop ends, to start the next row.
Common mistake: putting that new line inside the inner loop, which prints one value per line.

stations.name: Totalling a row
teaches: To total one row, loop across the columns with the row index held still.
sum(grid[r]) does the same job in one step, once you know which row you want.
Common mistake: letting the row index change inside the loop, which totals the wrong cells.

stations.name: Totalling a column
teaches: To total one column, loop down the rows with the column index held still.
The loop runs once for every row, so its range is len(grid).
Common mistake: using the number of columns as the range when travelling down a column.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: To search a grid, loop every cell and record the row and column where you found it.
A found flag, set before the loops start, says whether anything matched at all.
Common mistake: reporting only the row when the task asks where in the row it was too.

outcomeText.pr-l09-o1: know how to define a subprogram with def and how to call it
outcomeText.pr-l09-o2: understand how a parameter carries a value into a subprogram and how return carries one back out
outcomeText.pr-l09-o3: know how to write a subprogram that uses a variable of its own, and one that changes a shared variable

stations.name: Writing a procedure
teaches: def names a subprogram, and the indented block below it is what that subprogram does.
Nothing happens until the name is called, with brackets after it.
Common mistake: defining a procedure and never calling it, so none of it ever runs.

stations.name: Parameters
teaches: A parameter in the brackets lets whoever calls the subprogram pass a value in.
The value handed over is the argument, and inside it is used like any other variable.
Common mistake: giving the arguments in a different order from the parameters.

stations.name: Returning a value
teaches: return hands a value back to whatever called the subprogram.
The call can then be stored in a variable, printed, or used inside a bigger sum.
Common mistake: printing inside when the task says return, so nothing is handed back.

stations.name: Functions and procedures
teaches: A function returns a value; a procedure just does a job and returns nothing.
Both are subprograms, and in Python both are written with def.
Common mistake: calling something a function when all it does is print.

stations.name: Local and global
teaches: A variable made inside a subprogram is local: it exists only while that subprogram runs.
A global variable belongs to the main program, and global lets a subprogram change it.
Common mistake: expecting a local variable's value to survive after the subprogram ends.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: A subprogram may call another one, so a big job splits into small named steps.
Calling a function inside a loop lets one piece of code answer the same question many times.
Common mistake: repeating the same lines instead of writing one subprogram and calling it.

outcomeText.pr-l10-o1: know how to open a text file, read what is in it and close it again
outcomeText.pr-l10-o2: understand what write mode does to a file, and how append mode differs from it
outcomeText.pr-l10-o3: know how to split one line of a file into its separate fields and use them

stations.name: Reading a whole file
teaches: open(name, "r") opens a file for reading and hands back a file object.
.read() gives the whole file as one string, and .close() lets go of it when you are done.
Common mistake: opening a file that is not there, which stops the program with an error.

stations.name: Reading line by line
teaches: .readline() reads one line, while .readlines() gives a list of every line.
Each line still carries its newline, so .strip() tidies that off before you use it.
Common mistake: measuring a line before stripping it, which counts the newline as a character.

stations.name: Writing to a file
teaches: open(name, "w") opens a file for writing and empties whatever was in it.
.write() adds no newline of its own, so put a newline on the end of each line yourself.
Common mistake: using write mode on a file you meant to add to, which wipes it completely.

stations.name: Adding to a file
teaches: open(name, "a") is append mode: new text goes on the end and nothing already there is lost.
Use it whenever the lines the file already holds have to survive the run.
Common mistake: leaving the newline out, so the new text runs straight into the last line.

stations.name: Records in a file
teaches: A record is one line of the file, and its fields are the parts separated by a comma.
.split(",") breaks a line into a list of its fields.
Common mistake: splitting before stripping, which leaves a newline stuck on the last field.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Read the whole file first, close it, then work on the lines you are holding.
A program can read one file and write a second one in the same run.
Common mistake: looping over a file you have already closed, or reading and writing one file at once.

outcomeText.pr-l11-o1: know how to code a linear search and a binary search, and report the position each one finds
outcomeText.pr-l11-o2: understand how a bubble sort, an insertion sort and a merge sort each put a list in order
outcomeText.pr-l11-o3: know how to count the comparisons an algorithm makes, in order to compare two of them

stations.name: Linear search
teaches: A linear search checks each item in turn until it finds the one it wants.
It works on any list, in order or not, and reports the position or that nothing matched.
Common mistake: printing 'not found' inside the loop, once for every item that did not match.

stations.name: Binary search
teaches: A binary search looks at the middle item, then throws away the half that cannot hold the answer.
It only works on a list that is already in order.
Common mistake: not moving low or high, which leaves the loop checking the same middle forever.

stations.name: Bubble sort
teaches: A bubble sort compares each neighbouring pair and swaps them if they are the wrong way round.
Every pass pushes the largest remaining value to the end, so n items need up to n - 1 passes.
Common mistake: a swap that loses a value, because one side was overwritten before it was copied.

stations.name: Insertion sort
teaches: An insertion sort takes the next item and slides it back into place among the sorted ones.
The front of the list is always in order, and it grows by one item each time round.
Common mistake: overwriting an item instead of shifting it along to make room.

stations.name: Merge sort
teaches: A merge sort splits the list in half over and over, then merges the pieces back in order.
Merging compares the front of each sorted list and takes the smaller one each time.
Common mistake: stopping when one list runs out, instead of copying the rest of the other.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Count the comparisons to compare two algorithms fairly on exactly the same data.
Write the search or the sort out yourself, since sorted() and .index() hide the very steps being counted.
Common mistake: binary searching a list that was never sorted, which quietly gives the wrong answer.

outcomeText.pr-l12-o1: know how to code a presence check, a type check and a range check
outcomeText.pr-l12-o2: understand how a length check and a format check differ, and why the length is tested first
outcomeText.pr-l12-o3: know how to write a validation loop, and an authentication check that allows a set number of attempts

stations.name: Checking the input
teaches: A presence check refuses input that is empty once any stray spaces are stripped off.
A type check uses isdigit(), so text typed where a number was wanted cannot crash the program.
Common mistake: casting with int() before checking, which stops the program instead of rejecting the value.

stations.name: Range checks
teaches: A range check refuses anything that falls outside the allowed limits.
Inclusive limits need >= and <=, so the boundary values themselves are accepted.
Common mistake: using > where the rule says 'or more', which rejects a perfectly valid boundary.

stations.name: Length and format checks
teaches: A length check counts the characters with len(), against a minimum and a maximum.
A format check tests the pattern: which positions must be letters and which must be digits.
Common mistake: checking the pattern before the length, which can read past the end of the string.

stations.name: Keeping asking
teaches: A validation loop reads once, then repeats for as long as the value breaks a rule.
Saying which rule was broken makes the program far easier to use.
Common mistake: leaving the second input() out, so the loop tests the same bad value forever.

stations.name: Authentication
teaches: Authentication checks who the user is, usually with a username and a password.
An attempt counter lets a program lock the account after a set number of tries.
Common mistake: counting the attempts but never stopping, so guessing can carry on forever.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: Validate each value in its own loop before the program moves on to the next one.
A program that keeps going when one line of data is wrong is more useful than one that stops.
Common mistake: validating at the end, when the first bad value has already been used.

outcomeText.pr-l13-o1: know how SELECT and FROM choose the fields and the table a query reads
outcomeText.pr-l13-o2: understand how WHERE decides which records a query hands back
outcomeText.pr-l13-o3: know how to join conditions with AND and OR, and how to put results in order with ORDER BY

stations.name: SELECT and FROM
teaches: SELECT names the fields you want, and FROM names the table they live in.
SELECT * means every field, and with no WHERE every record comes back.
Common mistake: listing the fields in the wrong order, since results come out in the order you asked for.

stations.name: WHERE
teaches: WHERE filters the records, keeping only the ones whose condition is true.
Text to match goes inside quotes, and numbers do not.
Common mistake: leaving the quotes off text, so SQL looks for a field with that name instead.

stations.name: Comparing values
teaches: The comparisons are =, <>, >, <, >= and <=, and they work on numbers and on text.
'Longer than 45' is > 45, but '45 or longer' is >= 45.
Common mistake: using > where the question says 'or more', which loses the boundary record.

stations.name: AND and OR
teaches: AND keeps a record only when both conditions hold; OR keeps it when either one does.
Brackets make the meaning clear when AND and OR appear in the same WHERE.
Common mistake: using AND where the question means OR, which often gives no records at all.

stations.name: Sorting results
teaches: ORDER BY sorts the results by a field, smallest or earliest first.
DESC reverses that, so the largest or latest comes first instead.
Common mistake: putting ORDER BY before WHERE, when it always comes last.

stations.name: Putting it together
teaches: The clauses always come in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY.
Build a query one clause at a time and check what comes back at every step.
Common mistake: mixing up the quotes, so a word is read as a field name and the query finds nothing.

outcomeText.rp-l01-o1: know what is meant by defensive design when writing programs
outcomeText.rp-l01-o2: understand why input validation is necessary
outcomeText.rp-l01-o3: know a range of validation techniques used to write robust programs

stations.name: Defensive design
teaches: Designing a program so it can't be broken by mistakes or deliberate misuse.
Includes input validation, authentication, anticipating misuse and maintainable code.
Assume users will do something unexpected.

stations.name: Type check
teaches: Checks the data is the correct data type, such as a whole number rather than text.
Stops a program crashing when it tries to do maths with text.

stations.name: Range check
teaches: Checks data falls within acceptable limits, such as 1 to 3.
Anything outside the range is rejected.

stations.name: Presence check
teaches: Checks that some data has been entered.
Stops required fields, like a username, being left blank.

stations.name: Format and length checks
teaches: A format check makes sure data matches a pattern, such as DD/MM/YYYY or a postcode.
A length check makes sure data has the right number of characters, such as 11 digits for a mobile number.

stations.name: Whitelists and blacklists
teaches: A whitelist stores the only inputs a program should accept, e.g. A, B and C.
A blacklist stores inputs a program should reject, e.g. illegal characters in file names.
A string can be cast to a number after it has been checked.

outcomeText.rp-l02-o1: know what is meant by defensive design considerations
outcomeText.rp-l02-o2: know a range of problems that can occur when a program is running
outcomeText.rp-l02-o3: understand some authentication techniques programmers use

stations.name: Anticipating misuse
teaches: Thinking ahead about how users might accidentally or deliberately misuse a program.
E.g. typing text where a number is expected, or clicking a button many times.
Plan for every eventuality.

stations.name: When things go wrong
teaches: Even with valid input, a program can crash: dividing by zero, a lost connection, a printer out of paper, or a full disk.
Programmers use exception handling so the program copes instead of crashing.

stations.name: Authentication
teaches: Checking a user is who they say they are before they can use a system.
Usually a username and password.
Strong passwords are long and mix upper and lower case, numbers and symbols.

stations.name: Forgotten passwords and new users
teaches: A reset link or code can be sent to a registered email address or phone.
New users often confirm their email address before the account is activated.
Two-factor authentication adds a code sent to your phone.

stations.name: Bots and CAPTCHA
teaches: Bots are programs that fill in forms automatically, e.g. to make fake accounts or guess passwords.
CAPTCHA tests like 'I'm not a robot' are easy for humans but hard for bots.
Audio CAPTCHAs help users who can't see the images.

stations.name: Validate a password
teaches: It must be at least 10 characters long.
It must contain a digit and a letter.
It must not be one of the 100 most common passwords.

outcomeText.rp-l03-o1: know why creating code that is easy to read is important with large projects
outcomeText.rp-l03-o2: understand what programmers can do to make their code more readable
outcomeText.rp-l03-o3: understand how to refine algorithms to make them more robust

stations.name: Final challenge: good practice or bad?

outcomeText.rp-l04-o1: know four reasons why a program should be tested
outcomeText.rp-l04-o4: know what a syntax error is
outcomeText.rp-l04-o5: know what a logic error is

outcomeText.rp-l05-o1: understand that just because a program works doesn't mean it works for all inputs
outcomeText.rp-l05-o2: understand that test data should include normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous data

stations.name: Why test with different data?
teaches: A program that works for one input may still fail for others.
A test plan lists each test, the data used, the type of test and the expected result.
Good testing covers valid, invalid and erroneous inputs.

stations.name: Normal data
teaches: Typical, valid data that the program should accept.
For a school-age field from 11 to 19: 14.

stations.name: Boundary data
teaches: Valid data on the very edge of the accepted range.
For an age from 11 to 19: 11 and 19.
Boundaries are where programmers most often make mistakes, like < instead of <=.

stations.name: Invalid data
teaches: Data of the correct type, but outside the accepted range.
For an age from 11 to 19: 24 or -3.
The program should reject it.

stations.name: Erroneous data
teaches: Data of the wrong type that should be rejected.
For an age from 11 to 19: 'fourteen'.
Without a type check, erroneous data can crash a program.

stations.name: Test a comment box
teaches: A comment box allows up to 200 characters.
Test just under, exactly at, and just over the limit.
The program should show how many characters are left, or how many are over.

stations.name: Final challenge: sort the test data

outcomeText.rp-l06-o1: understand how robust programs are made
outcomeText.rp-l06-o2: know which lessons I'm secure on and which to revise

stations.name: Lesson 1: Input validation
teaches: Validation checks input is sensible before it's processed.
Type, range, presence, format and length checks.
Whitelists accept; blacklists reject.

stations.name: Lesson 2: Defensive design
teaches: Anticipating misuse: planning for mistakes and deliberate misuse.
Authentication: checking identity with passwords, 2FA and CAPTCHA.
Exception handling stops crashes.

stations.name: Lesson 3: Maintainability
teaches: Descriptive names, comments, indentation and white space.
Sub-programs split code into reusable parts.
Makes code easier to debug, update and maintain.

stations.name: Lesson 4: Testing and errors
teaches: Iterative testing: during development. Final testing: at the end, before release.
Syntax errors break the language's rules, so the code won't run.
Logic errors run but give the wrong result.

stations.name: Lesson 5: Test data
teaches: Normal: typical valid data.
Boundary: valid data on the edge of the range.
Invalid: right type, out of range. Erroneous: wrong type.

stations.name: Plan a 12-mark answer
teaches: What does it mean to produce a robust program?
Cover validation, authentication, anticipating misuse, maintainability and testing.
For each point, explain why it makes the program more robust.

outcomeText.sa-l01-o1: understand what the CPU of a computer does
outcomeText.sa-l01-o3: know the stages of the fetch-execute cycle
outcomeText.sa-l01-o4: know about other components of the CPU

stations.name: Purpose of the CPU
teaches: The CPU (central processing unit) processes data and instructions.
It does this by carrying out the fetch-decode-execute cycle, over and over.
It is sometimes called the brain of the computer.

stations.name: Stage 1: Fetch
teaches: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
The address is copied to the MAR, and the instruction is fetched from RAM into the MDR.
The PC is incremented, so it points to the next instruction.

stations.name: Stage 2: Decode
teaches: The instruction is now inside the CPU.
The control unit (CU) decodes it: it works out what the instruction means and what needs to be done.

stations.name: Stage 3: Execute
teaches: The instruction is carried out. Depending on the instruction, the CPU may:
fetch data from memory to use in a calculation, done by the ALU;
jump to another instruction, or write data from the accumulator back to RAM.

stations.name: The registers
teaches: Registers are tiny, very fast memory locations inside the CPU.
PC: address of the next instruction. MAR: address to fetch from or write to.
MDR: data fetched or to be written. ACC: results of calculations.

stations.name: Other CPU components
teaches: ALU (arithmetic logic unit): performs calculations and logical decisions.
CU (control unit): decodes instructions and sends signals to control how data moves.
Cache: fast memory for frequently used instructions and data.

outcomeText.sa-l02-o2: know the components of the von Neumann architecture

stations.name: John von Neumann
teaches: A Hungarian-American mathematician and computer scientist.
In 1945 he described a design for a computer that stores programs in memory.
Nearly all modern computers still follow his ideas.

stations.name: The stored-program concept
teaches: Instructions and data are both stored in the same main memory.
The CPU fetches instructions and data from memory, one at a time.
Loading a different program means the same computer can do a different job.

stations.name: Program counter and accumulator
teaches: Program counter (PC): holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
It increments during each fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Accumulator (ACC): holds the results of calculations done by the ALU.

stations.name: MAR and MDR
teaches: MAR (memory address register): holds the address of the data or instruction to be fetched or stored.
MDR (memory data register): holds the data or instruction fetched from memory, or to be written to it.
They work as a pair to move data between the CPU and RAM.

stations.name: Other architectures
teaches: Harvard architecture stores instructions and data in separate memories, with separate buses.
It lets an instruction and data be fetched at the same time.
It's used in many embedded systems and microcontrollers.

stations.name: Keywords
teaches: Every programming language has keywords: reserved words with a special meaning.
Python keywords include if, else, while, for, def, return, True and False.
You can't use a keyword as a variable name.

outcomeText.sa-l03-o1: understand three ways in which the speed of a CPU, and therefore a computer, can be increased
outcomeText.sa-l03-o2: know the units clock speed is measured in, and what overclocking does to heat

stations.name: Clock speed
teaches: The number of fetch-decode-execute cycles a CPU can carry out each second.
Measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is one cycle per second.
A 3.5 GHz CPU runs 3.5 billion cycles per second. Higher clock speed means more instructions each second.

stations.name: Overclocking and heat
teaches: Overclocking runs a CPU faster than its intended clock speed.
Faster CPUs produce more heat, so they need better cooling, like heatsinks and fans.
Too much heat can make a computer unstable or damage the CPU.

stations.name: Cache size
teaches: Cache is fast memory inside the CPU for frequently used instructions and data.
A bigger cache holds more, so the CPU makes fewer slow trips to RAM.
Cache comes in levels: L1 is fastest and smallest; L2 and L3 are bigger and a little slower.

stations.name: Number of cores
teaches: Each core is a processing unit that can fetch, decode and execute instructions on its own.
A quad-core CPU can process four instructions at the same time.
Doubling the cores doesn't always double the speed: software must be written to use them, and some tasks can't be split up.

stations.name: Single core, 2.5 GHz
teaches: 'Single core' means the CPU has one processing unit.
'2.5 GHz' means it runs 2.5 billion fetch-decode-execute cycles each second.
Exam answers should link each characteristic to its effect on performance.

stations.name: Units of speed
teaches: 1 kilohertz (kHz) = 1,000 cycles per second.
1 megahertz (MHz) = 1 million cycles per second.
1 gigahertz (GHz) = 1 billion cycles per second.

outcomeText.sa-l04-o1: understand what is meant by the term embedded system
outcomeText.sa-l04-o2: know several examples of embedded systems
outcomeText.sa-l04-o3: understand how an embedded system takes input, processes it and produces output

stations.name: What is an embedded system?
teaches: A computer system built into a larger device.
It has a dedicated function: it does one job, or a small set of jobs.
Examples: washing machines, microwaves, traffic lights and car engine management.

stations.name: Characteristics
teaches: Limited functions: runs one dedicated program.
Usually small, low power and cheap to mass produce.
Very reliable, and often has to respond in real time.

stations.name: Embedded systems everywhere
teaches: At home: washing machines, microwaves, smart thermostats, TVs and fridges.
Out and about: traffic lights, cash machines and car systems, like automatic lights and anti-lock brakes.
On you: fitness trackers and smartwatches.

stations.name: Input, process, output
teaches: Input: buttons, dials and sensors, such as a water temperature sensor.
Process: a microcontroller runs the program and makes decisions.
Output: motors, heaters, lights and displays.

stations.name: Programming embedded systems
teaches: The program is stored permanently in the device, often called firmware.
Embedded systems are often programmed in C or C++, which run fast and give close control of the hardware.
Some firmware can be updated, like a smart TV's software update.

stations.name: Embedded or general purpose?
teaches: A general-purpose computer, like a laptop, can run many different programs.
An embedded system is built in to one device and does one dedicated job.
Some devices blur the line, like smart TVs that run apps.

stations.name: Final challenge: spot the embedded system

outcomeText.ss-l01-o1: know the purpose and functionality of operating systems
outcomeText.ss-l01-o2: know the different types of user interface and the features of each

stations.name: What is systems software?
teaches: Software is split into two kinds: systems software and application software.
Systems software runs the computer itself: the operating system and utility programs.
Application software is what the user runs to do a job: a browser, a game, a word processor.

stations.name: What the OS does
teaches: It manages the processor, sharing it between programs.
It manages memory, deciding what is held where.
It manages files, users, and input and output devices.
It provides a user interface so people can work with the machine.

stations.name: Graphical user interface
teaches: A GUI uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer.
It is easy to learn, and needs no commands to be memorised.
It uses more memory and processing power than a text interface.

stations.name: Command line interface
teaches: A CLI is text only: the user types commands.
It uses very little memory and processing power.
It is powerful and easy to automate with scripts, but commands must be learned.

stations.name: Menu driven and voice
teaches: A menu driven interface offers a set of choices, one screen at a time: a cash machine, a ticket machine, an old MP3 player.
It is very easy to use, but slow, and you can only do what the menus allow.
A voice interface listens for spoken commands: useful hands free, and for users who can't use a screen, but it mishears and needs a quiet room.

stations.name: Choosing an interface
teaches: Think about the user: their skill, their situation and what they need to do.
Think about the hardware: a device with no screen can't use a GUI.
Exam answers need the choice, the characteristic and the reason.

outcomeText.ss-l02-o1: know what is meant by the term multitasking
outcomeText.ss-l02-o2: understand how the operating system manages memory
outcomeText.ss-l02-o3: understand the need for device drivers

stations.name: Multitasking
teaches: Multitasking means several programs appear to run at the same time.
A single processor core can only run one instruction at a time.
The OS switches between programs so quickly that it looks simultaneous.

stations.name: Sharing the processor
teaches: Each process gets a short time slice, then the OS interrupts it and moves to the next.
Saving one process and loading the next is called a context switch.
Important jobs can be given priority, so they run sooner.

stations.name: Managing memory
teaches: Every running process needs space in RAM, and the OS decides where it goes.
The OS keeps processes apart, so one crashing program can't damage another.
When RAM fills up, data that isn't being used is moved to virtual memory on the disk.

stations.name: Virtual memory
teaches: Virtual memory is space on secondary storage used as extra RAM.
Data not being used right now is swapped out to disk to make room.
It is far slower than RAM, so it is a last resort, not a plan.

stations.name: Device drivers
teaches: A driver is software that lets the OS communicate with a piece of hardware.
Each device needs a driver written for it, and for that operating system.
Without the right driver, the device either doesn't work or loses its special features.

stations.name: Updates and plug and play
teaches: Plug and play means the OS recognises a device and finds a driver automatically.
Drivers are updated to fix faults, improve speed and close security holes.
A faulty driver can crash the whole machine, because drivers run with high privileges.

outcomeText.ss-l03-o1: understand what is meant by user management
outcomeText.ss-l03-o2: understand the ways an operating system manages files

stations.name: User accounts
teaches: Each person gets an account: a username, a password and their own settings and files.
The OS checks the password before letting anyone in. This is authentication.
Accounts mean the same machine can be shared without anyone seeing anyone else's work.

stations.name: Access levels
teaches: An access level decides what a user may do with a file: nothing, read it, or read and change it.
Give each user the least access their job needs.
The OS checks the level every time a file is opened.

stations.name: Groups and profiles
teaches: Setting permissions for thousands of people one at a time is impossible, so users are put into groups.
A permission set on a group applies to everyone in it.
A profile holds a user's settings, so their desktop follows them to any machine on the network.

stations.name: Files and folders
teaches: The OS stores data as files, and organises them in folders.
Folders sit inside folders, forming a hierarchy that starts at the root.
A path describes the route to a file, for example Documents\Computing\1.5\notes.docx.

stations.name: What the OS does with files
teaches: It creates, opens, renames, moves, copies and deletes files.
It records where each file is physically stored, and how much space is free.
It shows a tidy hierarchy to the user, even though the blocks may be scattered across the disk.

stations.name: File extensions
teaches: The extension is the part after the dot: .docx, .jpg, .mp3, .exe.
It tells the OS which program should open the file.
Changing the extension doesn't change what is inside the file.

stations.name: Final challenge: lock down the network
What is utility software?
teaches: Utility software is systems software that maintains and protects the computer.
It works on the machine itself, not on the user's documents.
Examples: encryption, defragmentation, compression, backup and anti-malware.

stations.name: Encryption
teaches: Encryption scrambles data using a key, turning plaintext into cyphertext.
Without the key it is meaningless, so a stolen file or laptop gives nothing away.
The same key, or a matching one, decrypts it back to the original.

stations.name: Defragmentation
teaches: Over time, files get split into pieces scattered across a disk. This is fragmentation.
The read/write head then has to jump about to collect one file, which is slow.
A defragmentation utility gathers each file into one run and groups the free space together.

stations.name: Compression
teaches: A compression utility makes files smaller so they use less space and send faster.
Lossless compression restores the original exactly: used for text, programs and archives.
Lossy compression throws data away for a much smaller file: used for photos, music and video.

stations.name: Backup and updates
teaches: A backup utility copies files so they can be restored after loss, theft or ransomware.
A full backup copies everything; an incremental backup copies only what has changed since last time.
Update utilities keep the OS and drivers patched, closing security holes.

stations.name: Choosing the right utility
teaches: Match the utility to the problem: slow mechanical disk, risk of theft, files too large, data loss.
Exam answers need the utility, what it does, and why it fits the situation.
